alert: PaprikaUnexpectedPrune expr: increase(paprika_prune_total[5m]) > 5 labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Application {{ $labels.app }} pruned {{ $value }} resources in 5m" Troubleshooting Drift "OutOfSync but the resource looks identical" Check for Kubernetes-defaulted fields that differ from the desired manifest: # Compare desired (from release snapshot) vs live kubectl get <kind> <name> -n <ns> -o json | jq '.spec' Common causes: env value: null in the chart (fixed in current version) initialDelaySeconds: 0 on probes (fixed) Resource quantity formatting (500m vs 0.5) (fixed) API group collisions (Knative Service vs core Service) (fixed) "Pruned but the resource should exist" Check if the resource was removed from the chart: # Check the release's manifest snapshot kubectl get configmap <snapshot-name> -n <ns> -o json | jq -r '.data["manifests.yaml"]' | grep <name> If the resource should persist, annotate it with paprika.io/prune: "false". "Missing but the resource exists" Check for API group collisions — the desired object might resolve to thewrong GVR. The CachedGVRResolver should handle this; if it persists, checkthe controller logs for GVR resolution errors. Architecture Details Diff Engine ScalableDiffEngine (internal/engine/scalable_diff.go): label-selectordiff computation, apiVersion-qualified resource keys, generated-childexclusion, cluster-scoped GVR handling. DiffEngine (internal/engine/diff.go): basic diff engine (namespace-widescan), resourceEqual, specContains, mapContains — null-as-absent handling,Kubernetes default omission. CachedGVRResolver (internal/engine/gvr_resolver.go): discovery API withcaching, knownGVRs fast path, pluralization fallback. Prune pruneStaleResources (internal/controller/pipelines/release_controller.go):runs after successful applyAllDocuments, lists live resources by GVR withpaprika labels, deletes ownerless resources not in the desired set. Key Formats Resource key: apiVersion/Kind/namespace/name (e.g.serving.knative.dev/v1/Service/deephost/deephost-hydra) Desired key: built from parsed manifests with the same format, usingthe release namespace as fallback for namespaced resources Live key: built from listed live objects with the same format

title: Manage delivery across Kubernetes clusters
description: Register deployment targets, configure direct or satellite connections, and understand cluster inventory and application placement.
text: Multi-Cluster Orchestration Paprika combines cluster registrations, application placement, and observedhealth into one fleet. A satellite in each remote cluster watches local stateand sends compact reports to the central control plane over an outbound HTTPSconnection. The first authorized report registers the cluster and adds itsapplications to the existing fleet views. Each Stage also references a Cluster resource that describes how theoperator should connect to its deployment target. Cluster Modes The Cluster CR supports three connection modes: Mode Use Case in-cluster The operator runs inside the target cluster and uses its own service account. direct The operator connects to a remote API server using a kubeconfig stored in a Secret. agent A satellite reports observed state through an outbound connection. Deployment through the existing apply agent additionally requires a reachable agent endpoint. Direct access to GKE with Workload Identity The Paprika manager image includes a client-go credential helper. It obtainsshort-lived Google application-default credentials from the manager pod'sWorkload Identity and does not require gke-gcloud-auth-plugin or a serviceaccount key. Bind the manager's Kubernetes service account to a dedicated Googleservice account, then grant that identity only the GKE discovery and targetKubernetes RBAC permissions needed for the registered cluster. Ensure themanager can reach the target API endpoint and that the kubeconfig contains itsverified CA certificate. This is separate from spec.provider cloud inventorycredentials and from satellite authentication. Place a kubeconfig in the direct Cluster's referenced Secret, with the usualcluster, CA, context and user entries. Its user authentication block is: exec: apiVersion: client.authentication.k8s.io/v1 command: /manager args: [gke-exec-credential] interactiveMode: Never Client-go refreshes the short-lived token before expiry. Restrict who can writethe Cluster and its kubeconfig Secret: a kubeconfig exec entry is executableconfiguration in the manager pod, not merely a credential. Verify target RBAC,network reachability, remote reads and a migration hook before using theconnection for production promotions. Satellite reports alone do not provethat this direct deployment transport works. For a live, read-only check from the manager pod, obtain the expected targetendpoint and namespace UID independently from the cloud provider and targetcluster, then run: kubectl -n paprika-system exec deployment/paprika-controller-manager -c manager -- \ /manager fleet-direct-probe --cluster-namespace paprika-system \ --cluster-name vocus-prod --target-namespace sfh-vocus-prod \ --expected-server https://EXAMPLE.gke.goog --system-ca \ --expected-namespace-uid EXPECTED_UID Use the actual manager deployment, Cluster name, target endpoint and namespaceUID for the installation. The DNS endpoint mode uses the image's system CAroots; it refuses custom CA files, proxies and insecure TLS. For an endpointusing a pinned private CA, replace --system-ca with--expected-ca-sha256 and the SHA-256 of its CA bytes. The command uses theregistered kubeconfig and the same client-go configuration path as releasereconciliation, reads the target namespace, and returns JSON containing theregistration and Secret identities, the target namespace UID and observationtime. It rejects a registration or Secret changed during the read. Its outputdoes not include tokens, kubeconfig contents or credential errors. Compare theidentities and resource versions with fresh management-cluster reads beforeusing the result; successful observation does not authorize a deployment orprove write permissions, migration hooks or ongoing connectivity. Satellite Onboarding Install the central chart and CRDs from a build containing satellite support.The API and operator serve /api/satellite/report; expose that route at thecentral API origin. Satellite authentication uses a token scoped to one clusterregistration and is independent of browser or MCP authentication. For each physical cluster, choose a unique, stable central name. A satellitederives the physical cluster's identity from the kube-system namespace UID.The control plane pins that UID on the first report and rejects a differentcluster using the same registration. Create one random token and provision it in both environments. The centralSecret must be named <cluster-name>-satellite-token and carry the labelpaprika.io/satellite-cluster: <cluster-name>. The satellite chart referencesan existing local Secret; keep the token out of values files, command flags,and version control. # Replace these values with the intended contexts and central API origin. PAPRIKA_CONTROL_CONTEXT=control-plane PAPRIKA_SATELLITE_CONTEXT=edge-eu PAPRIKA_CONTROL_NAMESPACE=paprika-system PAPRIKA_SATELLITE_NAMESPACE=paprika-satellite PAPRIKA_CLUSTER_NAME=edge-eu PAPRIKA_CONTROL_URL=https://paprika.example.com PAPRIKA_IMAGE_TAG=replace-with-immutable-build-tag paprika_satellite_tmp="$(mktemp -d)" chmod 700 "$paprika_satellite_tmp" trap 'rm -rf "$paprika_satellite_tmp"' EXIT openssl rand -hex 32 | tr -d '\n' > "$paprika_satellite_tmp/token" chmod 600 "$paprika_satellite_tmp/token" kubectl config use-context "$PAPRIKA_CONTROL_CONTEXT" kubectl config current-context kubectl -n "$PAPRIKA_CONTROL_NAMESPACE" create secret generic \ "$PAPRIKA_CLUSTER_NAME-satellite-token" \ --from-file="token=$paprika_satellite_tmp/token" kubectl -n "$PAPRIKA_CONTROL_NAMESPACE" get secret \ "$PAPRIKA_CLUSTER_NAME-satellite-token" kubectl config current-context kubectl -n "$PAPRIKA_CONTROL_NAMESPACE" label secret \ "$PAPRIKA_CLUSTER_NAME-satellite-token" \ "paprika.io/satellite-cluster=$PAPRIKA_CLUSTER_NAME" kubectl -n "$PAPRIKA_CONTROL_NAMESPACE" get secret \ "$PAPRIKA_CLUSTER_NAME-satellite-token" --show-labels kubectl config use-context "$PAPRIKA_SATELLITE_CONTEXT" kubectl config current-context kubectl create namespace "$PAPRIKA_SATELLITE_NAMESPACE" kubectl get namespace "$PAPRIKA_SATELLITE_NAMESPACE" kubectl config current-context kubectl -n "$PAPRIKA_SATELLITE_NAMESPACE" create secret generic \ paprika-satellite-token --from-file="token=$paprika_satellite_tmp/token" kubectl -n "$PAPRIKA_SATELLITE_NAMESPACE" get secret paprika-satellite-token helm template paprika-satellite charts/satellite/ \ --namespace "$PAPRIKA_SATELLITE_NAMESPACE" \ --set "controlPlaneURL=$PAPRIKA_CONTROL_URL" \ --set "cluster.name=$PAPRIKA_CLUSTER_NAME" \ --set "cluster.namespace=$PAPRIKA_CONTROL_NAMESPACE" \ --set token.existingSecret=paprika-satellite-token \ --set "image.tag=$PAPRIKA_IMAGE_TAG" kubectl config current-context helm upgrade --install paprika-satellite charts/satellite/ \ --namespace "$PAPRIKA_SATELLITE_NAMESPACE" \ --set "controlPlaneURL=$PAPRIKA_CONTROL_URL" \ --set "cluster.name=$PAPRIKA_CLUSTER_NAME" \ --set "cluster.namespace=$PAPRIKA_CONTROL_NAMESPACE" \ --set token.existingSecret=paprika-satellite-token \ --set "image.tag=$PAPRIKA_IMAGE_TAG" \ --wait --timeout 5m kubectl -n "$PAPRIKA_SATELLITE_NAMESPACE" get deployments,pods kubectl --context "$PAPRIKA_CONTROL_CONTEXT" \ -n "$PAPRIKA_CONTROL_NAMESPACE" get cluster "$PAPRIKA_CLUSTER_NAME" -o yaml If the satellite namespace already exists, omit its creation. No Paprika CRDsare required in the remote cluster: standard Deployments, StatefulSets, andDaemonSets supply application observations. When the remote cluster also hasPaprika Applications, the satellite watches their status and uses thoseapplication identities. For a pre-existing agent registration, declare the satellite token explicitly: apiVersion: clusters.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: Cluster metadata: name: edge-eu namespace: paprika-system spec: displayName: Edge Europe mode: agent satellite: tokenSecretRef: name: edge-eu-satellite-token key: token Newly onboarded clusters appear in the cluster board and their applicationsjoin fleet queries automatically. An existing direct registration can optinto reporting by adding spec.satellite.tokenSecretRef; its kubeconfig anddeployment connection keep working. A newly onboarded agent Cluster canlater use mode: direct with a kubeconfigSecretRef to enable centraldeployment orchestration while retaining its satellite observations.The in-cluster registration continues to use the control plane's own serviceaccount for inventory. Management Policies A Cluster declares the ceiling of what Paprika may do to it, followingCrossplane's managementPolicies vocabulary. The field is on the Cluster, noton the satellite block, because the ceiling applies to every transport: adirect kubeconfig and a satellite report are two ways to reach the samecluster, and a read-only cluster is read-only either way. apiVersion: clusters.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: Cluster metadata: name: edge-eu namespace: paprika-system spec: mode: agent managementPolicies: [Observe] # observations only; nothing is written satellite: tokenSecretRef: name: edge-eu-satellite-token key: token Policy Permits Observe Reading inventory, drift, health and capacity. Never writes. Apply Creating and updating managed resources, including sync hooks. Prune Deleting managed resources dropped from the desired manifest set. Delete Deleting managed resources when a Release is deleted. Without it, release cleanup orphans the workloads. SelfHeal Re-applying drift and rolling back a degraded release without an operator asking. Rollout Shifting traffic through canary, blue-green, A/B and mirror strategies. * Every policy this build knows. Three rules decide the effective set: Unset means full management. A Cluster with no managementPolicies grantseverything, so every existing registration keeps working. An explicitly empty list grants nothing. managementPolicies: [] is theway to say "registered, but manage nothing"; omitting the field is not. A Stage narrows, never widens. spec.stages[].managementPolicies on anApplication, and spec.managementPolicies on a standalone Stage, areintersected with the Cluster ceiling. A stage asking for * on anObserve-only cluster gets Observe. Two failures are deliberate. A policy read that fails for any reason other than"no such registration" is reported rather than degraded to full management —assuming a ceiling away on an API blip is exactly the write an observe-onlycluster is meant to prevent. And a withheld action parks the work instead offailing it: the Release stays in Promoting with a PromotionPolicyWithheldcondition naming the refused action, and rechecks every five minutes. Wideningthe ceiling lets it proceed without a retry. status.satellite.reportedPolicies records the satellite's last reported localclaim. status.satellite.effectivePolicies intersects that claim with theCluster ceiling and expands *; it is unknown until the first report. Theclaim is an observation, not an authorization check or grant. The satellite'sactual Kubernetes permissions still apply. A direct connection uses the Cluster and Stage ceilingsseparately, so it can have different permissions from an Observe-only satellite.A spec change recomputes the satellite's effective set from its last claim evenwhile the satellite is disconnected. Autonomy and Disconnection spec.satellite.autonomy records what the satellite is supposed to do while itcannot reach the control plane: Mode While connected While disconnected ObserveOnly Reports state; the control plane reconciles. Nothing converges until the link returns. Failover (default) The control plane reconciles. The satellite takes over after failoverTimeout (default 2m). Delegated The satellite reconciles; the control plane supplies desired state and observes. Nothing changes, because the satellite was already the reconciler. A satellite reconciles what it was told to apply. Every bundle the controlplane pushes down the link is applied and then remembered in a ConfigMap(paprika-satellite-bundles) in the satellite's own namespace, and the autonomyloop re-applies those bundles on an interval (--satellite-autonomy-interval,default 30s). That is deliberately narrower than the control plane's releasemachinery: a satellite enforcing the last known-good bundle through an outage isuseful, while a satellite reconciling a release history it cannot see would notbe. The handover is one-directional and time-gated. Failover waits forfailoverTimeout of failed deliveries before reconciling, so a control-planerestart does not produce two reconcilers at once. After local work, a reconnectreports OverrideHeld for two minutes before returning to Connected: thecontrol plane needs to see that the cluster changed underneath it before thesatellite claims to be a quiet follower again. Delegated is not an overridecase; a satellite acting there is the arrangement. status.satellite.operatingState carries the result: Connecting, Connected,Autonomous, OverrideHeld, or Disabled for a disabled registration. The satellite's ServiceAccount needs write verbs for whatever its applicationsdeploy. The chart grants reads plus the bundle store and nothing else, so anapply is refused until rbac.extraClusterRoleRules grants your kinds. Capacity and Node Pools The satellite sums node status.allocatable and scheduled, non-terminal podcontainer requests on every report, and reads metrics.k8s.io when the clusterhas it. The result lands in status.satellite.capacity; usedKnown says whetherusage was actually measured, so a cluster without metrics-server reportsrequests and allocatable and marks usage unavailable rather than claiming idle. kubectl -n paprika-system get cluster edge-eu -o json \ | jq '.status.satellite.capacity, .status.satellite.nodePools' Node pools are derived from the provider's pool label (vke.vultr.com/node-pool,cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool, eks.amazonaws.com/nodegroup,kubernetes.azure.com/agentpool), falling back tonode.kubernetes.io/instance-type. The provider type is detected from nodeproviderID prefixes and copied into status.provider.type, so a cluster thecontrol plane cannot dial still shows its pools. Provider-API enrichment —autoscaler bounds, plan sizes — still requires spec.provider credentials and areachable API; status.provider.state stays NotConfigured until that happens. Capacity for an agent-mode cluster is served from the satellite report. Adirect cluster keeps the live read even when it also reports through asatellite, because a live read is fresher than a heartbeat. Stream Transport Set stream.enabled=true on the satellite chart to keep one bidirectionalConnect stream open instead of posting each report. Reports still travel in thesame JSON document the POST transport sends, validated and fenced by the samecode — the transport changes how the bytes arrive, never what the control planeaccepts. The link is off by default because the POST path is what every existingsatellite runs. The link's reason to exist is the reverse direction. With a live link, a releasethat targets an agent-mode cluster can apply its rendered bundle down thesatellite's own outbound connection, so the cluster needs no inbound route andthe control plane keeps no kubeconfig for it: control plane ──task: apply bundle──▶ satellite ──server-side apply──▶ cluster API ◀──result: 12 applied── The satellite runs the bundle through the same apply path as the inbound agent,so both transports produce the same result. A failed apply over a live link isreported and not retried through the agent endpoint: the cluster may havehalf the bundle applied, and a second attempt would race the satellite's own. Deployability is a runtime question, not a field. A registration withmode: agent, a satellite block and no inbound endpoint can observe butcannot apply until the link attaches. Target resolution asks the dispatcher fora live link and refuses the target when there is none; the release then failswith "connect the satellite" instead of trying an endpoint that was never goingto answer. The link is an HTTP/2 bidirectional Connect stream, so it needs an HTTP/2server. A cleartext http:// endpoint is accepted for loopback only (a sidecaror a local run), and the satellite speaks prior-knowledge h2c there. Go'stransport does not attempt h2c on its own, so a plain http:// clientnegotiates HTTP/1.1 and the stream never opens. The collector hands the sender areport rather than encoded bytes, because the two transports frame differently:the POST path sends gzip with Content-Encoding, the link puts the JSONdocument inside a protobuf message. In split mode the links live in the API server's pod and the reconciler runs inanother, so the control plane needs a way to bridge them. Enablesatellite.internalDispatch.enabled on the chart: it creates a shared token,has the API server serve /internal/satellite/{links,dispatch} on an in-clusterport, and points the controller at that address. The listener is a separateaddress rather than a path on the public API mux, because an apply endpointreachable from the internet would let anyone holding the port push manifestsinto satellites. It refuses every request when no token is configured, and thecontroller fails at startup if it is given an address without one. Leaving thevalue off keeps split mode working exactly as before: agent clusters fall backto the inbound agent endpoint, which a satellite-only cluster does not have. One limit still applies: the link accepts only reports and applies. Theresource-tree, log and live-diff reads that need a command channel are not wiredto it yet. That limit has a consequence for deletion: the agent transport has no deletepath, so deleting a Release that targeted one leaves its workloads running. Therelease object still deletes and logs which stage kept its resources. Blockingthe finalizer instead would make such a release impossible to remove, and theworkloads belong to the cluster either way. State Transport and Reconnects One satellite Deployment runs per cluster. Shared Kubernetes watches maintaina local cache for nodes, pods, namespaces, supported workloads, and optionalPaprika Applications. The initial report contains a complete applicationsnapshot; later reports send changed applications and deletion keys, withcluster inventory as an aggregate. Reports are batched every two seconds bydefault, gzip-compressed, and sent over a reusable HTTP connection. Idleclusters send a heartbeat every 30 seconds. Each report carries a session ID and sequence number. Retries preserve thesame report identity, allowing the control plane to acknowledge duplicatedelivery without repeating its effects. Reconnects begin with a fresh snapshotso deleted applications do not remain in the central view. The current protocolbounds each uncompressed report to 1 MiB and each cluster to 2,000 observedapplications. Cluster reports persist in Cluster.status.satellite, so a control-planerestart reconstructs the view from Kubernetes. If heartbeats stop, observationsremain visible with unknown health and sync state. The cluster becomesUnhealthy after the greater of three health-check intervals andconnectionTimeout (90 seconds with defaults).If you increase the chart's heartbeatInterval beyond this window, alsoincrease the central Cluster's spec.healthCheck.interval so idle clustersremain current between heartbeats. The chart uses a single replica and a Recreate deployment strategy to avoidoverlapping reporters during upgrades. It exposes only the local probe port;the central control plane does not require inbound network access to thesatellite. The service account grants get, list, and watch for the watchedresources and get on /version. It does not need access to Secrets orpermission to apply application manifests. Application Identity Across Clusters Application identity defaults to namespace and application name. Instances ofproduction/payments on multiple clusters become one logical application withone placement per cluster. staging/payments remains a separate application.The fleet retains each placement's health and connection state and aggregatesthe logical application using the least healthy placement and combinedresource counts. Paprika Applications report their known drift; nativeworkloads report unknown sync state because they have no Paprika desired-statecomparison. Aggregate drift counts are shown where reported; the placementtable shows health and connectivity. To group differently named instances within a namespace, setapp.paprika.io/identity to the same valid DNS subdomain on their PaprikaApplications or workloads: metadata: name: payments-eu namespace: production labels: app.paprika.io/identity: payments Namespaced identity also applies to this explicit label; it cannot mergedifferent namespaces. Observations must agree on their declared project beforethey can join one application. A central Application retains its release andcontrol metadata while gaining remote placements. Applications discovered onlythrough satellites are visible as observations and have no central mutationcapabilities. Private CAs and Credential Rotation For a private HTTPS CA, create a ConfigMap containing ca.crt in the satellitenamespace and set ca.existingConfigMap (and ca.key if necessary). Thesatellite adds that CA to its trust store. HTTPS is required for remoteendpoints; plain HTTP is accepted only for loopback development. The mounted token is read for each report, so a Secret update can rotate itwithout restarting the satellite. Update the central token and then the localtoken; reports retry through the short mismatch window. Disabling the centralCluster or removing its central token Secret stops report authorization. Deployment Transport Satellite reporting supplies fleet observation. Deploying to a remote targetcontinues to use the existing direct kubeconfig connection or reachableagent apply endpoint. The registered Cluster's spec.mode is authoritative;a Stage reference cannot override it with a different mode. For directdeployment, the registration must provide spec.kubeconfigSecretRef pointingto a central Secret whose kubeconfig key contains the remote kubeconfig.Set key: kubeconfig explicitly. Install and grant that deployment transportthe permissions required by its manifests separately from the read-onlysatellite. Satellite onboarding alone does not grant remote deploymentpermissions. For example, enable deployment on an onboarded cluster while retaining itssatellite reports: apiVersion: clusters.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: Cluster metadata: name: edge-eu namespace: paprika-system spec: displayName: Edge Europe mode: direct kubeconfigSecretRef: name: edge-eu-kubeconfig namespace: paprika-system key: kubeconfig satellite: tokenSecretRef: name: edge-eu-satellite-token key: token Remote hook lifecycles, trafficRouter changes, live podMetrics analysis,desired-resource drift checks, and Release resource cleanup use the Stage's target cluster and the sameregistered kubeconfig credentials as workload apply. The inbound agenttransport supports manifest apply; these other operations require directtransport and report an explicit error when configured against an agenttarget. When the current deployment target cannot supply live resource reads, theApplication records DiffUnavailable, marks health unknown and sync incomplete,and pauses drift-triggered self-healing. It retains last-known resource statusuntil the target becomes readable again; a missing remote resource is neverinferred from the control plane's local cluster. This is a property of thetransport, not a reconcile failure: a satellite target logs the reason at debuglevel and reports it through the condition, so a fleet of satelliteapplications does not fill the log with a limitation that will not change untilthe target is registered as direct. Read and apply resolve separately for the same reason. Drift resolution asks fora read transport; apply resolution asks whether an apply can reach the targetright now, including over a live satellite link. Answering the apply questionfirst makes a briefly absent link look like a drift failure. The console follows the same rule. A resource tree, live manifest, event listor pod log is read from the cluster the application's active release deploysto, resolved through the release's stage to its Cluster registration. Adirect cluster is read through one cached client per cluster. An agentcluster has no API the control plane may dial, so live children, node detail,logs and events are reported as unavailable rather than answered from themanagement cluster — the names usually exist on both, so reading the wrong onelooks like success. The status-derived half of those views (managed resources,sync status, reported health) still renders. Release deletion keeps the cleanup finalizer when its Stage or targettransport cannot be resolved. Preserve Stage and Cluster registrations andtheir credentials until Release deletion completes so cleanup can reach theresources on the correct cluster. Registering a Cluster Create a Cluster resource: apiVersion: clusters.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: Cluster metadata: name: prod-cluster namespace: paprika-system spec: displayName: Production mode: direct server: https://prod-cluster.example.com kubeconfigSecretRef: name: prod-kubeconfig namespace: paprika-system key: kubeconfig healthCheck: interval: 30s timeout: 10s connectionTimeout: 30s For agent mode: apiVersion: clusters.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: Cluster metadata: name: edge-cluster namespace: paprika-system spec: displayName: Edge mode: agent satellite: tokenSecretRef: name: edge-cluster-satellite-token key: token Kubeconfig Secret For direct mode, store a valid kubeconfig in a Secret: apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: prod-kubeconfig namespace: paprika-system type: Opaque stringData: kubeconfig: | apiVersion: v1 kind: Config clusters: - name: prod-cluster cluster: server: https://prod-cluster.example.com certificate-authority-data: <base64-ca> users: - name: prod-user user: token: <token> contexts: - name: prod context: cluster: prod-cluster user: prod-user current-context: prod Permissions the Remote Credential Needs The user in that kubeconfig is the identity Paprika acts as on the targetcluster, so it needs the permissions for what Paprika does there. Beyond theaccess your applications' own manifests require, capacity meters read two morekinds, both read-only: apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: ClusterRole metadata: name: paprika-capacity-reader rules: # KubernetesCapacity sums status.allocatable across nodes and container # requests across pods. It never writes either, and never reads the node # proxy or the eviction subresource. - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["nodes", "pods"] verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"] Bind it to the remote credential's subject with a ClusterRoleBinding. Withoutit, a capacity read reports DATA_STATE_FORBIDDEN for that cluster rather thanfailing the request — the meter goes dark, nothing else does. That state isdistinct from DATA_STATE_ERROR on purpose: FORBIDDEN means the read reachedthe cluster and was refused, which is a grant you can make, while ERROR coversevery other way a read fails. Whichever it is, the number beside it is zero:Paprika never renders a figure it cannot substantiate. Grant exactly these verbson exactly these resources; cluster-admin is never the fix for a capacitypermission error. For an in-cluster (mode: in-cluster) target the chart-managed manager rolealready carries them, so nothing extra is needed. Capacity Providers Where a capacity number comes from is configuration, not code. Two customresources describe it: CapacityProvider names an implementation and configures it. Theimplementation is a registry key this build ships, not an arbitrary string —an unknown key is rejected at admission. DataProviderBinding attaches a provider to a scope: Namespace,Cluster, Project or Global. Two implementations ship today: spec.provider Supplies Reads Configuration KubernetesCapacity allocatable, requested Nodes and Pods, core API none MetricsServer used metrics.k8s.io none What a Default Install Already Has The chart ships a KubernetesCapacity provider bound at Global scope in therelease namespace, so allocatable and requested capacity work with nothing toconfigure, plus a MetricsServer provider bound the same way so used populateswherever the metrics.k8s.io aggregated API exists. On clusters withoutmetrics-server installed the provider reports NOT_AVAILABLE with a fixedreason — it never fails the read — and the meter completes itself ifmetrics-server is installed later. Turn the defaults off with--set capacity.defaultProvider.enabled=false and--set capacity.metricsServer.enabled=false if you would rather manage themyourself. Completing the Meter A scope may have more than one provider bound to it, and that is how a meter iscompleted rather than replaced: each provider's readings are merged, and asuccessful measurement is never overwritten by another provider's failure or byits "I don't supply that field". KubernetesCapacity gives allocatable andrequested; MetricsServer gives used; together they are one meter. apiVersion: providers.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: CapacityProvider metadata: name: metrics-server namespace: paprika-system spec: provider: MetricsServer --- apiVersion: providers.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: DataProviderBinding metadata: name: metrics-server-global namespace: paprika-system spec: providerRef: kind: CapacityProvider name: metrics-server scope: kind: Global Binding a second provider to one scope is supported. Binding the sameprovider to one scope twice is rejected — it says nothing the first binding doesnot. Scope Precedence Bindings resolve most-specific-first, independently for each provider: Namespace > Cluster > Project > Global So a Global binding is a fleet-wide floor, and a Cluster-scoped binding forthe same provider overrides it for that cluster alone — you never have to removethe broad binding to special-case a narrow one. Two scope levels are guarded, because both can speak for someone else: A Global binding may only be created in the control plane's own namespace(the release namespace, which the deployments pass as --operator-namespace).It applies to the whole fleet, so a tenant-created one would repoint whatevery other tenant sees. A Namespace binding may only name the namespace it lives in. Namespace isthe most specific level, so one naming another tenant's namespace would winthe chain inside it. scope.selector is present in the CRD but not yet honoured, and is rejected atadmission rather than silently ignored. Name the scope with scope.name. Pointing Capacity at Prometheus Later A Prometheus provider — capacity plus RED signals, over PromQL — is the nextimplementation planned, and it is why this is a binding model rather than aconfig flag. When it lands, moving one cluster onto it is a CapacityProvidernaming it and a Cluster-scoped DataProviderBinding; the GlobalKubernetesCapacity binding stays where it is and keeps serving every othercluster. Nothing already bound changes meaning. Neither shipped implementation takes any configuration, and both reject anon-empty spec.config at admission rather than ignoring it, so a stale ortypo'd config cannot pass unnoticed. Whatever an implementation does accept,a literal credential is never part of it: token- and password-shaped fields arerefused at admission, at any nesting depth. Referencing a Cluster from a Stage A Stage can reference the Cluster by name: apiVersion: pipelines.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: Stage metadata: name: my-app-prod namespace: paprika-system spec: name: prod ring: 3 templates: - my-app-template cluster: name: prod-cluster namespace: paprika-system The cluster block in ApplicationPromotionStage supports the same referenceand can be used inline in an Application. Use one stage for each target: metadata: name: payments namespace: production spec: stages: - name: dev ring: 1 - name: prod-eu ring: 2 cluster: name: edge-eu namespace: paprika-system - name: prod-au ring: 3 cluster: name: edge-au namespace: paprika-system Add these stages to the Application's source and delivery configuration.Paprika creates Stage resources named payments-dev, payments-prod-eu,and payments-prod-au in production. Only one ring deploys at a time, in ascending ring order, with declarationorder breaking ties so a ring can hold parallel stages. status.currentStagerecords what is live now. When that stage's release completes and nothing itdeployed is degraded, a stage with autoPromote: true starts the next ring asa new Release; the final ring simply rests. autoPromote is read from the ringbeing left, so a verified ring decides whether the next one may start withoutan operator. The next ring deploys the bundle the previous ring verified. For an inlineapplication the manifest source lives on the Release rather than on theApplication, so the promoted Release inherits it from the completed one insteadof rebuilding from the Application, which has no manifests of its own torebuild from. A new source revision restarts at the first ring: a commit made while the fleetsits on production still passes through the rings that verify it. A manual syncretries the ring an operator is looking at rather than restarting the pipeline.Multi-ring releases are named per stage (payments-release-<hash>), so eachring is its own Release object; single-ring applications keep their existingrelease name. The dev stage defaults to thecontrol plane's in-cluster target; the two production stages resolve theirrespective registrations. Register edge-eu and edge-au with directcredentials to run the full deployment lifecycle on both clusters. Full Example apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: prod-kubeconfig namespace: paprika-system type: Opaque stringData: kubeconfig: | apiVersion: v1 kind: Config clusters: - name: prod cluster: server: https://prod.example.com certificate-authority-data: LS0t... users: - name: deployer user: token: eyJhbG... contexts: - name: prod context: cluster: prod user: deployer current-context: prod --- apiVersion: clusters.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: Cluster metadata: name: prod namespace: paprika-system spec: displayName: Production mode: direct server: https://prod.example.com kubeconfigSecretRef: name: prod-kubeconfig namespace: paprika-system key: kubeconfig --- apiVersion: pipelines.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: Application metadata: name: my-app namespace: paprika-system spec: source: type: helm chart: repo: https://charts.example.com name: my-app version: 1.2.3 strategy: Rolling syncPolicy: Auto stages: - name: dev ring: 1 - name: prod ring: 2 cluster: name: prod namespace: paprika-system Rollouts on a Remote Cluster A Rollout runs advanced strategies against one workload. By default thatworkload is on the control plane's own cluster; spec.cluster points therollout at a registered cluster instead: apiVersion: rollouts.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: Rollout metadata: name: checkout namespace: checkout spec: cluster: name: edge-eu namespace: paprika-system target: kind: Deployment name: checkout strategy: type: Rolling The Rollout object stays on the control plane; the Deployment, ReplicaSets,Services and traffic routes it manages are read and written in the namedcluster. An agent cluster is refused: a rollout reads and writes workloads itcannot reach through an outbound link, and running it against the control planeinstead would report success while the real workload never moved. Progression for a remote rollout comes from its own requeues, not from watchevents: the controller's Owns watches are on the control plane, so aReplicaSet becoming ready in the remote cluster does not wake it early. Thedefault requeue interval is the latency floor. Fanning Out with an ApplicationSet An ApplicationSet with a clusters generator produces one Application perregistered cluster, so a fleet addition is a registration rather than an editto every application: apiVersion: pipelines.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: ApplicationSet metadata: name: checkout namespace: checkout spec: generators: - clusters: namespace: paprika-system selector: matchLabels: tier: production template: metadata: labels: region: "{{.region}}" placement: "{{.name}}" project: default source: type: git repoURL: https://github.com/example/checkout targetRevision: main path: deploy stages: - name: "{{.name}}" ring: 1 cluster: name: "{{.name}}" namespace: "{{.namespace}}" namespace is the namespace holding the registrations, which is usually thecontrol plane's rather than the application's; it defaults to theApplicationSet's own namespace. selector matches labels on the Clusterobject or in its spec.labels. names lists registrations explicitly andresolves them the same way. Each registration contributes these parameters: Parameter Value name Cluster resource name, and the cluster.name a stage needs namespace Namespace holding the registration, for cluster.namespace mode direct, agent, or in-cluster server API server URL when the registration sets one provider Detected cloud provider, when one was detected region, tier Convenience copies of those two labels label_<key> Every spec.labels entry, with characters outside [A-Za-z0-9_] replaced by _ Disabled clusters are skipped: generating an Application that can only failfills the console with placements that will never converge. A name listed innames that has no registration still generates an Application, which thenfails where an operator can see it. Generator parameters feed the Application name, so changing them (adding agenerator parameter, moving a set to a selector) renames the generatedApplications and replaces them. That is a real rollout, not a no-op. Fleet Scale Characteristics The satellite fleet view is rebuilt by merging every registration's observationsinto the local snapshot. Two measurements bound what that costs, taken frominternal/fleet benchmarks (go test ./internal/fleet -bench MergeSatellite): Fleet shape Merge cost 10 clusters x 20 apps, one shared app 0.4 ms 100 clusters x 20 apps, one shared app 3.2 ms 500 clusters x 20 apps, distinct apps 64 ms, 80 MB allocated The merge runs on the query path: the first fleet query after any report thatchanges observations pays it, and every query after that is cached until thenext change. On a live stack with 50 registrations x 20 applications, a QueryFleetMap atrest measured p50 5 ms / p95 7 ms, and a query immediately after a single statuschange measured p50 18 ms / p95 66 ms before the window existed. With coalescingin place, the same query under a 150-patch burst (50 registrations, three roundsapplied in parallel) measured p50 5 ms / p95 23 ms / max 36 ms. Observation changes are coalesced at the satellite source into at most onepublished generation per 250 ms window, so the merge is bounded at roughly fourper second regardless of how fast the fleet reports. The cost is that a readercan see a view up to 250 ms old, which is invisible in a dashboard and farcheaper than one rebuild per report. The window lives in the source rather thanthe reader on purpose: the reader's contract is that a changed generation isvisible on the next call, and callers rely on it. ListClusters with includeCapacity has a different cost profile: capacity isgathered per registration, so a fleet where many registrations cannot be dialledpays that fan-out. With 50 unreachable test registrations it measured p50 23 ms/ p95 232 ms, against 5 ms for the map query over the same fleet. Observation Store The bottleneck at a thousand applications is the status object: every reportrewrites Cluster.status.satellite.applications, which is ~300 KB at that size.internal/obsstore is the provider seam for moving those observations out of theKubernetes API: --satellite-observation-store Behaviour kubernetes (default) Cluster.status is the store. Nothing changes. memory Observations go to an in-process store; useful for tests. redis Observations go to Redis (--satellite-redis-addr, optional --satellite-redis-password-file, --satellite-redis-db). The chart exposes the same choice: satellite: observationStore: provider: redis redis: addr: redis:6379 existingSecret: redis-auth # optional; key `password` db: 0 Selecting redis without an address fails the render rather than starting acontrol plane whose store can never connect. Selecting any provider other thankubernetes also requires deploymentMode=split: the fleet source is wired tothe store in the split API server only, and enabling it in monolith mode wouldwrite observations to a store nothing reads, emptying the satellite view. Thechart refuses that combination instead of producing it. One Redis key per cluster plus an index set, so a report rewrites only its owncluster's observation rather than contending on one shared value. Writes arebest effort: the report is already durable in status, and failing the reportwhen the store is down would make a store outage look like a satellite outage. The store records the report exactly as the satellite sent it, not a projectedview. Projection rules change with the fleet model, and a store holdingyesterday's projection would turn a rules rollout into a data migration. With a provider selected, the report baseline — the list a delta merges onto —is read from the store, the merged list is written back as a full observation,and status.satellite keeps only the summary fields plus session/sequencefencing. A store that cannot be read fails the report rather than mergingagainst an unknown baseline. The sequence fence still reads status deliberately: session and sequence aresmall, so concurrency control never depends on the store being reachable. Cluster Health The cluster controller periodically health-checks registered clusters. Check status with: kubectl get cluster -n paprika-system Cluster health describes the latest connection or satellite report status.Deployment operations resolve the Stage's transport separately; a missing,disabled, unsupported, or failing transport stops the Release operation withan error. The In-Cluster Registration The chart installs a Cluster with mode: in-cluster (named<release>-in-cluster) so the cluster the control plane runs in appears onthe cluster board. A stage with no cluster ref deploys in-cluster, and thefleet index resolves that empty ref to this registration — which is whatlets list_clusters count the applications that run there. On each health check the controller also gathers inventory — node andready counts, pod counts, namespace count, distinct regions and zones, andkubelet versions — into status.inventory, and detects the cloud providerfrom node providerID prefixes (vultr://, gce://, aws://,azure://). Disable the self-registration with --set cluster.self.enabled=false. Cloud Provider Enrichment spec.provider adds what the provider's own API knows: the managedcluster's provider-side ID and region, and node pools with plan names andautoscaler bounds — things Kubernetes node objects do not carry. spec: provider: type: auto # auto | vultr | gke | eks | aks clusterId: "" # provider's identifier: VKE UUID, EKS/GKE/AKS name region: "" # EKS region / GKE location / AKS location project: "" # GCP project, or Azure resource group subscriptionId: "" # Azure subscription (aks only) credentialsSecretRef: # optional where ambient identity exists name: cluster-cloud-creds key: credentials # default type: auto resolves the provider from node providerIDs. Even with nocredential configured, status.provider reports the detected provider andnode pools derived from node labels (vke.vultr.com/node-pool,cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool, eks.amazonaws.com/nodegroup,kubernetes.azure.com/agentpool), with state NotConfigured. API-enrichedpools — autoscaler bounds included — only appear once the provider answers. Every pool also carries allocatableCpuMillis and allocatableMemoryBytes:the sum of its nodes' status.allocatable, i.e. the pool's real capacity forworkloads. Provider APIs generally report pool shape (plan, autoscalerbounds) without live node counts or sizing — Vultr v2 returns count: null —so figures the provider does not report are filled from the node-derived setby name. A pool the provider reports but no node matches keeps its zeroes:provisioned but empty is real data, not a gap. Credentials per provider The referenced Secret key holds a provider-specific document: Provider Document Ambient alternative vultr the API key, as a plain string none — Vultr has no workload identity eks JSON {"access_key_id","secret_access_key","session_token"} SDK default chain: IRSA, pod identity, node role gke Google credential JSON — a workload identity federation external_account config or a service_account key application default credentials (GKE workload identity) aks JSON {"tenant_id","client_id","client_secret"} or {"tenant_id","client_id","federated_token_file"} AZURE_* workload-identity environment The credential document's shape is checked before use: a Google document isonly accepted as service_account, external_account orimpersonated_service_account, and every provider failure maps to a state(NotConfigured, Forbidden, NotAvailable, Error) with a sanitizedreason — credential material and endpoint details never appear in status. Matching rules when clusterId is empty: vultr and eks match thecluster whose published apiserver endpoint equals the one Paprika dials —which cannot work for mode: in-cluster (kubernetes.default.svc is nevera published endpoint), so set clusterId for the self-registration.gke/aks always require clusterId (admission-enforced).

title: Connect the observability gateway
description: Configure Paprika Observe providers and authenticated MCP access for querying metrics, logs, traces and saved dashboards.
text: Observability Gateway The observability gateway is Paprika's MCP surface for querying observabilitybackends — logs, metrics, and traces — through pluggable connectors. It runsas its own microservice (its own Deployment in split mode, its own --mode inthe shared binary) and exposes: https://<paprika-host>/observe/mcp on the same hostname and TLS identity as the console (/mcp keeps serving thefleet surface). Gateway tokens carry the paprika-observability audience andthe paprika:observe scope for reads. When Insights is configured, the separatepaprika:insights:write scope enables saved-query and dashboard authoring,subject to the user's Insights RBAC permissions. A token minted for the consoleor fleet MCP surface is not replayable here and vice versa — even though allsurfaces share the deployment's HMAC token secret. For request budgets, scope boundaries, repeatable local checks, profiling and liveacceptance, see validation guidance. Architecture Claude/Codex → https://paprika.example.com/observe/mcp (HTTPRoute, /observe) │ h2c ▼ Deployment/<release>-observability-gateway │ mcp.Server (RoutePrefix /observe, ScopeObserve + optional authoring, │ console resource extensions disabled, own embedded │ consent page at /observe/consent) ▼ internal/observabilitygateway.Backend │ per call: get ObservabilityProvider CR │ (namespace/name) → resolve credentialsSecretRef ▼ connector.New(type).Query(...) (stateless; config travels per-request) │ ▼ prometheus / loki / tempo / otlp (plain HTTP, no vendor SDKs) internal/observabilitygateway/connector — the connector framework:Connector interface (Descriptor / ValidateConfig /Query), a dup-rejecting Registry, signal/state/sentinel vocabulary thatdeliberately parallels internal/clusterprovider and internal/dataprovider(state strings OK/NotConfigured/NotAvailable/Error/Forbidden; sentinelsErrForbidden / ErrNotConfigured / ErrUnsupported / ErrNotAvailable). Connector errors never echo endpoints, credentials, or response bodies intotool results — users get fixed sentences, detail goes to the gateway log(clusterprovider sanitize discipline). Unsupported query shapes return a StateNotAvailable result plus an errorwrapping ErrUnsupported; the backend returns the result and logs the error. Query backpressure and provider bulkheads Paprika Observe now admits short bursts through bounded queues instead ofrejecting every query when execution is busy: MCP per-principal token buckets (50 requests/s, burst 100) permit up to 8queued requests per authenticated user and 64 globally, each waiting at most2 seconds. A canceled MCP call does not execute after disconnect. The observability backend permits 4 concurrent queries globally and2 concurrent queries per provider, with at most 32 global waiters and 8per-provider waiters. Admission waits no longer than 5 seconds, while eachexecution retains its 30-second budget and any earlier caller deadline.These are the defaults. The --observability-query-* flags and theobservabilityGateway.capacity chart values change them, and the gatewayrefuses to start on a combination that cannot work (see below). Insights permits 16 concurrent query executions and up to 64 queuedrequests waiting at most 2 seconds. query_dashboard executes distinctsaved queries once and propagates the request deadline to providers. Overfull queues still return an explicit capacity error (429 / resourceexhausted); holding a connection indefinitely would consume worker memory,create head-of-line blocking and hide provider outages. All limits are per process. Multiple replicas do not provide a single globalcluster-wide queue; shared ordering across pods requires a separate durablescheduler, which is not appropriate for synchronous MCP requests. Query results are returned synchronously. Queuing does not change OAuth scopes,provider RBAC, saved dashboard versions or query timeout/error semantics. End-to-end capacity A dashboard query passes eight hops between the browser and the provider. Eachrow gives the hop's default limit, where it is configured, and what a callersees when the hop is full. The defaults are the values in code. A changed flagor chart value replaces them, and the gateway validates the combination atstartup. # Hop Limit (default) Configured in When full, the caller sees Retry 1 Browser scheduler (createQueryScheduler, ui/src/features/insights/query.ts) 4 queries in flight per viewer, maximum 16 Code only Nothing is sent; further widgets wait in the local queue n/a 2 Browser replay (capacityRetryDelay, ui/src/features/insights/client.ts) A 429 on /query, a read or a conditional write is replayed up to 3 times, waiting Retry-After seconds. A wait over 10 s is not retried Code only After the replays fail the widget shows "Query failed" with a Retry button (ui/src/features/insights/charts.tsx) Manual 3 Console API proxy (insightsProxyRequestHandler, internal/api/insights_proxy.go) No admission limit. Response-header timeout 25 s (transport) and a 28 s request budget (insightsProxyRequestHandler); the header timeout cuts in first if Insights sends no headers. The console's connection cap is --api-max-conns (128) Code; --api-max-conns An unreachable or slow Insights gets 502 "Insights service is unavailable" Yes, with backoff 4 Insights admission (acquireQuery, internal/insights/server.go) 16 executing, 64 waiting, 2 s wait Code only; a later slice adds flags /query: 429 "too many active queries; retry shortly" with Retry-After: 1. Dashboard queries: a per-signal rate_limited error inside a 200 response, not an HTTP 429 (dashboardProviderError) Yes, after Retry-After 5 Gateway HTTP admission (observabilityAdmissionPool, limitObservabilityProtocolRequestsWith) Intake 8 (waiters cover all pool capacity), MCP work 4 (up to 32 waiting, the budget queue), catalog 4 and dashboards 2 (each up to its own size waiting). One deadline of 1 s covers the intake and pool waits --observability-http-* flags; chart observabilityGateway.capacity.http* 429 "observability gateway is at its request limit; retry later", Retry-After: 1, Cache-Control: no-store Yes, after Retry-After 6 Gateway MCP rate limit (mcpRatePerSecond, mcpRateBurst, mcpRateQueueWait in internal/api/mcp/ratelimit.go) 50 requests/s, burst 100 per principal. Queue: 8 per principal, 64 in total, each waiting at most 2 s Code only 429 "rate limit queue is full; retry shortly", Retry-After: 1 Yes, after Retry-After 7 Gateway execution budget (DefaultBudgetConfig, executionBudget.begin, internal/observabilitygateway/budget.go) 4 executing across providers, 2 per provider. Queued: 32 across providers, 8 per provider. The admission cap is 36 (concurrency + queue). Per provider, the budget holds 2 running and 8 waiting, so 36 is reachable only across at least four providers (see below). A waiter holds its place for at most 5 s. Each execution has a 30 s budget that starts when it is admitted --observability-query-* flags; chart observabilityGateway.capacity.query* Queue full, reported as resource_exhausted. On REST (/observe/api/query) that is 429 temporarily_unavailable with Retry-After: 1 (writeDashboardError). On MCP it is an error result with code resource_exhausted and no retry hint, text from operationalToolErrorText. Queue wait expired, or the 30 s budget used up, is a deadline error: 504 on REST, "tool execution timed out" on MCP 429: yes, after Retry-After. 504: yes, with backoff, since the earlier attempt may have used provider time 8 Backend connector (internal/observabilitygateway/connector/…) Per-connector client timeouts: Shorted queryTimeout 10 s (connector/shorted), Uptime queryTimeout 20 s (connector/uptime), PostgreSQL connect 5 s (connector/postgresql). The 30 s budget applies to all of them Code only A provider failure is a sanitized error state in the result, or 502 server_error on REST. Insights passes a gateway 504 through as 504 without Retry-After (observeHTTPError) Yes, with backoff What each hop's wait costs. Edge (hops 5 and 6). The intake and pool waits share one deadline of--observability-http-admission-wait (1 s by default), measured from the startof the handler. A request that is refused there has waited at most that long.The MCP rate queue (hop 6) runs after edge admission and adds at most 2 s. Budget (hop 7). A query waits at most --observability-query-queue-wait(5 s) for a slot. The 30 s execution budget starts when the query is admitted,so after a wait its execution time is still a full 30 s. Over REST the dashboardhandler applies its 30 s to the whole request, queue wait included. Per MCP request, worst case: admission wait + 2 s rate queue + queue wait +30 s execution. At defaults that is 38 s. The validator requires the sum tostay at or below 40 s, which leaves 5 s to read, serialise and write theresponse before the 45 s HTTP write timeout. Per Insights /query, worst case: the console proxy ends a UI query at28 s, whatever the gateway is doing, and its 25 s response-header timeout cutsin earlier when Insights has sent no headers. Insights' own write timeout is30 s (cmd/paprika-insights/main.go), so the proxy's 28 s decides. Inside thatbudget Insights holds a query for at most 2 s at hop 4, and each providerconnection it opens has a 20 s budget (observe_mcp.go). Disconnects. Once a request's body has been read, a client that leaveswhile the request waits for its pool is noticed at once, because the serverthen watches the connection. A request that is still waiting for an intakeslot, before its body is read, is noticed only when that wait ends, which isat most the admission wait. A body larger than the classification limit isread only in part, so the same applies to it. REST POST bodies(/observe/api/query, /observe/api/explore) are read the same way as MCPbodies, so a departed client is noticed at the same point for both. What is coupled to what. Dashboard pool is min(2, --observability-query-concurrency). It servesquery_dashboard and render_dashboard, which run nested data requests, andit does not follow the per-provider flag. 36 is not one provider's capacity. The edge admits 36 data requests, butthe budget holds 2 running and 8 waiting per provider. With one provider, 10are admitted and the rest get resource_exhausted. The budget holds all 36only when load spreads across at least four providers (4 x 10 = 40). Listing shares a bulkhead. Every Insights Observe query first listsproviders, under one shared catalog bulkhead (2 running and 8 waiting, plusa global slot). So 36 simultaneous listings run 10 and refuse 26. Provider listing (ListProviders) runs under the catalog pseudo-provider'sbulkhead, which is sized by the per-provider flag. Setting--observability-query-provider-concurrency=1 therefore also runs listings oneat a time. Catalog pool is the work pool's size by default. Each Insights providerquery opens two MCP connections, resolve and data (observability_provider.go).Each connection's initialize, notifications/initialized and tools/listrequests, and the list_observability_providers call, are classified ascatalog requests (isObservabilityCatalogEnvelope). Only the data tools/calluses the work pool. Keep the catalog pool large enough for handshakes whilequeries run. Intake is held only while a request body is read and classified, thenreleased before the pool wait. It is not a cap on all in-flight requests. Itsdefault is twice the work pool. Work pool and its edge queue. The work pool may be sized up to queryconcurrency + queue, beyond which the budget would refuse first. Its edgewaiters equal the budget queue. A request that arrives while 4 are running and32 are waiting is refused at once, which is the edge's 37th. Intake's waiterscover all pool capacity, so intake does not refuse first. Each request stillwaits at most --observability-http-admission-wait (1 s) for a slot. Theexperiment behind this (the Insights-shaped burst) models only this HTTP edge,with a fixed 500 ms provider time and no execution budget, so it shows the edgeadmitting 36 queries in time. Real provider times and per-provider limitsturn part of a burst into 429s, as the listing and per-provider notes abovedescribe. With the queue at 0 the workpool fails fast, which matches the budget. Catalog and dashboard pools keepwaiters equal to their size. Sizing a board. Let N be the number of distinct queries on a dashboard,R the refresh interval in seconds and T the mean provider time per query inseconds (measure T on your provider). The board asks for about N / R queries persecond. One provider can serve about (provider concurrency) / T of those persecond, which is 2 / T at defaults, and all providers together about 4 / T.Keep N / R comfortably below the capacity of the providers the board uses. Eachviewer can run 4 queries at once (hop 1), so several viewers multiply the demandon the shared gateway. Duplicate queries on one dashboard run once(query_dashboard executes distinct saved queries once), so N counts distinctqueries. Changing capacity. Raise the budget first, then the pools, or set pools to 0and let them follow. The gateway refuses these combinations at startup, namingthe flag to change: query concurrency between 1 and 1024; provider concurrency between 1 and queryconcurrency (0 means min(2, concurrency)); queue between 0 and 65536; provider queue between 0 and the queue. With queue0, set the provider queue to 0 too, because its default of 8 would exceed it; queue wait above 0 and below the 30 s request timeout; admission wait between 0 and 5 s, and no longer than the queue wait; admission wait + 2 s + queue wait + 30 s at most 40 s, leaving 5 s before the45 s write timeout; queue wait and admission wait are either zero or at least 1 ms; work pool no larger than query concurrency + queue; dashboard pool no larger than query concurrency; every pool between 0 and 65536, where 0 follows its rule. Units in config files. Flags, environment variables and the chart useduration strings such as 5s. A --config file uses the flag names as keys: observability-query-queue-wait: 5s observability-http-admission-wait: 1s A bare integer such as 5 is read as nanoseconds, so it is refused at startup(below 1 ms) with a message that suggests a unit. In the chart, httpAdmissionWaitaccepts 0, "0s" or a unit-bearing string; 0 rejects at once. The gateway logs the resolved budget and pools at startup, with the source ofeach derived value (Observability gateway capacity). The chart renders thesevalues as --observability-* arguments on the gateway container(charts/chart/templates/observability-gateway/deployment.yaml). The MCP surface Fifteen provider tools, all read-only and requiring paprika:observe: Tool Purpose list_observability_providers List ObservabilityProvider CRs (name, type, state) get_observability_provider One provider's descriptor (signals it supplies) query_logs LogQL query (loki/otlp connectors) query_metrics PromQL instant/range query (prometheus/otlp) query_traces TraceQL search or trace_id fetch (tempo/otlp) query_records Bounded typed rows from Shorted, Uptime or read-only PostgreSQL list_metric_names Enumerate a metrics provider's metric names (prefix/limit filters) list_metric_series Bounded metric series/label sets in a time range; supports approximate cardinality inspection list_label_names Label names — globally or on one metric (prometheus/loki/tempo tags) list_label_values One label's values, optionally constrained to a metric get_metric_metadata One metric's type/help/unit (prometheus /api/v1/metadata) list_trace_services Service names a tempo provider has spans for list_provider_types The provider-type catalog (library view) describe_provider_type One type's config schema + onboarding walkthrough validate_provider Offline syntax validation of prospective provider configuration Metric, label and trace-service exploration accepts optional RFC 3339 startand end bounds. Series enumeration defaults to the trailing thirty minutes;explicit windows are limited to 31 days. A bounded series sample is not aglobal active-series count. Insights consumes the supported Prometheus/Tempotools through this MCP endpoint using the signed-in user's delegated access. Insights also uses query_records for application and SQL dashboards. Theseproviders can project numeric columns through query_metrics; inventories donot become historical series unless the source supplies timestamps. See therepository example library and theShorted, Uptime andPostgreSQL adapter contracts. When Insights is configured, the same MCP endpoint additionally exposes: Tool Required scope Purpose list_insights_providers paprika:observe Discover provider IDs used in saved UI documents get_insights_schema paprika:observe Discover canonical dashboard, widget or saved-query JSON Schema and examples list_saved_queries, get_saved_query paprika:observe Read saved queries and their ETags list_dashboards, get_dashboard paprika:observe Read shared dashboards and their ETags query_dashboard paprika:observe Execute a saved dashboard and read compact, versioned live signals with optional variable overrides create_saved_query, create_dashboard paprika:observe + paprika:insights:write Create a new shared document without replacing an existing ID update_saved_query, update_dashboard paprika:observe + paprika:insights:write Update a document using the exact ETag from its latest read patch_saved_query, patch_dashboard paprika:observe + paprika:insights:write Edit selected fields and dashboard widgets by ID, atomically against the current ETag All document tools also enforce the user's global insights read/write RBAC.The authoring scope grants no fleet operations or provider configuration.Existing paprika:observe tokens remain read-only, including on refresh;authoring requires a fresh native OAuth grant that explicitly requests the newscope. An omitted-scope authorization request retains the read-only default.Create saved queries before dashboards that reference them, and preserve typedparameters and bindings. A stale update returns a conflict: reread the documentand reconcile the intended edit instead of issuing a wildcard overwrite. Start authoring with get_insights_schema (kind: dashboard, widget, orsaved_query). It returns the deployed Insights service's full JSON Schema,examples and semantic-validation notes. For small changes, preferpatch_saved_query or patch_dashboard: nested objects merge, null removes afield, and arrays replace in full. Dashboard widgets use widget_edits withadd, update or remove operations addressed by stable widget ID. A batch isvalidated and persisted once; any invalid edit or ETag conflict leaves thedocument unchanged. See the targeted authoring contract. The tools use the same persistent Insights service as the UI. Open workspacesrefresh externally saved changes while protecting unsaved local drafts.Provider credentials and the Insights service token never enter tool responses.query_dashboard resolves the same saved-query bindings as the UI and executesidentical panel queries once. Its structured result contains latest readings,range summaries, a bounded trace sample, document ETags and explicitmissing/error/truncation states. History is opt-in; service overrides nevermodify saved defaults. Data availability is not a service-health verdict.See the dashboard query contract forlimits, examples and interpretation.See the Observe plugin for connectionand authoring guidance. The five exploration tools answer in the backend's own JSON envelope({"status":"success","data":[...]} for prometheus/loki, {"tagNames":[...]}/ {"tagValues":[...]} for tempo) so a caller can explore a backend and thenquery what it found without learning a gateway dialect. Exploration is anoptional connector capability (connector.Explorer) implemented per provider,each mapping the generic kinds onto its own native discovery mechanism: Provider metric_names label_names label_values metric_metadata trace_services prometheus /api/v1/label/__name__/values (+ prefix/limit) global /api/v1/labels, or per-metric via /api/v1/series union global or per-metric series union /api/v1/metadata — loki — /loki/api/v1/labels /loki/api/v1/label/x/values — — tempo — /api/search/tags /api/search/tag/x/values — service.name tag values aws-cloudwatch-metrics ListMetrics (optional namespace arg; paginated) dimension-name union from ListMetrics dimension-value union for a label — (no metadata API) — aws-cloudwatch-logs DescribeMetricFilters — — — — aws-xray — — — — GetServiceGraph (trailing 30 min) aws-cloudtrail — static LookupAttributes catalog — — — gcp-cloudmonitoring metricDescriptors.list (starts_with prefix filter) descriptor labels[].key union — (values not enumerable) exact descriptor passthrough — gcp-cloudlogging logMetrics.list — — — — vultr-monitoring static catalog (account_bandwidth, instance_bandwidth_in/outgoing_bytes) static instance_id/label/region/status live GET /v2/instances union static type/help/unit per catalog metric — gcp-cloudtrace, otlp, mock* — → StateNotAvailable — — — — * mock implements every kind from a fixed synthetic catalog (e2e stayshermetic). A provider type answering StateNotAvailable returns a fixedsentence naming the missing capability — data, not an error. The optionalnamespace argument is read by the CloudWatch metrics connector only. Tool args take provider as namespace/name. start/end are RFC3339(default: last 30 minutes); limit defaults vary by connector. OAuth 2.1 + PKCE, RFC 7591 dynamic client registration, and RFC 9728/8414discovery all work exactly like the fleet MCP surface, under /observe/*: GET /.well-known... — served at /observe/.well-known/oauth-protected-resourceand /observe/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server (the 401 challenge'sresource_metadata points there; the host-root well-knowns remain theconsole surface's). Consent: browsers are redirected to /observe/consent, a minimalself-contained page embedded in the gateway binary. Unifying it with thebranded console consent page is follow-up work. Configuring providers ObservabilityProvider is a namespaced CR (groupobservability.paprika.io): apiVersion: observability.paprika.io/v1alpha1 kind: ObservabilityProvider metadata: name: prometheus namespace: paprika-e2e spec: type: prometheus # prometheus | loki | tempo | otlp | # gcp-cloudlogging | gcp-cloudmonitoring | gcp-cloudtrace | # aws-cloudwatch-logs | aws-cloudwatch-metrics | # aws-xray | aws-cloudtrail config: endpoint: http://kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus.monitoring:9090 # credentialsSecretRef: # optional # name: grafana-cloud-token # namespace/key optional (default: CR ns, "credentials") spec.config is opaque per-connector JSON, validated at admission by theconnector itself (webhook rejectInlineCredentials refuses literaltoken/password keys anywhere in the document; put credentials in a Secret). spec.credentialsSecretRef document: nil = no auth; otherwise the secretdata[key] is sent as Authorization: Bearer <value>, or HTTP Basic when itcontains user:password. The referenced Secret must be labelledobservability.paprika.io/credentials=true. The gateway's service accountcan read far more than provider credentials, and whoever writes a providerchooses both the Secret and the endpoint it is sent to, so only Secretsopted in by label are ever read; any other reference reportsNotConfigured. CreateObservabilityProvider labels the Secret it creates;label Secrets you create yourself:kubectl label secret <name> -n <ns> observability.paprika.io/credentials=true. A Secret in another namespace (credentialsSecretRef.namespace) is read onlyfor a caller authorized for providers in that namespace. The status proberacts for no caller, so such a provider reports NotConfigured in statuswhile authorized queries still work. endpoint (absolute http(s) URL) is the one universal config key; unknownkeys fail validation (typo fail-fast). Optional keys: headers — map of extra request headers (≤16 entries, ≤4 KiB combined):vendor tenancy like Loki/Grafana/Mimir X-Scope-OrgID. Operator-declaredheaders win Authorization collisions (documented + tested). insecureSkipTLS — bool, for self-signed in-cluster backends only (neveroff-cluster; per-config client so verified/unverified TLS sessions nevershare connection pools). step — prometheus-only range-query step override (Go duration, >0, ≤1h;otherwise derived as max(10s, span/250)). Connector specifics type signals query behavior prometheus metrics PromQL; range (start+end) → /api/v1/query_range with computed step, instant otherwise loki logs LogQL → /loki/api/v1/query_range; limit default 100, max 1000 tempo traces trace_id → /api/traces/<id>; TraceQL → /api/search otlp logs, metrics, traces Generic OTLP/HTTP retrieval proxy: GET <endpoint>/v1/{logs,metrics,traces} with trace_id/start/end/limit params when set gcp-cloudlogging logs Query = Cloud Logging advanced filter; empty → probe (entries:list, 1 entry) gcp-cloudmonitoring metrics Query = Monitoring filter; window required (defaults to trailing hour); empty → probe (metricDescriptors, 1 row) gcp-cloudtrace traces trace_id → one trace; Query = optional list filter; empty → probe (1 trace) aws-cloudwatch-logs logs Query = CloudWatch filter pattern (empty = all events); config logGroup required; probe = 1 event aws-cloudwatch-metrics metrics Query = metric name in config namespace (required); period derived from window (clamped 60–3600s, Average/Sum/Maximum); empty → probe (ListMetrics) aws-xray traces trace_id → BatchGetTraces; Query = X-Ray filter expression (empty = all); probe = summaries, trailing 10 min aws-cloudtrail audit Query = comma-separated Key=Value lookup attributes (e.g. EventName=RunInstances,EventCategory=Activity), empty = all; limit ≤ 50; probe = 1 event mock metrics, logs, traces Synthetic in-process backend for load tests, demos and e2e — no network egress. Config knobs (all optional, bounded): series, pointsPerSeries, labelsPerSeries, logEntries, traces, spansPerTrace (payload shape), latencyMs (context-aware synthetic latency), failEvery (deterministic stable error subset — every Nth distinct query string), seed (deterministic generator seed; identical query + seed = identical data) Perf testing with the mock connector hack/obsloadgen drives the gateway's MCP surface with N concurrent clients(one self-signed paprika-observability token each — distinct subjects sothe per-subject rate limiter binds no client but its own), andtask perf:obs-* wraps the loop for the kind perf stack: task perf:obs-seed COUNT=50 # seed varied mock providers (idempotent) task perf:obs-load SECS=60 CLIENTS=32 RPS=5 task perf:obs-profile SECS=30 # combined load + pprof capture task perf:obs-metrics # gateway /metrics + kubectl top Grafana Cloud uses the same three native connectors with the Grafana Cloudendpoint and an API token as credentials, e.g.: spec: type: prometheus config: endpoint: https://prometheus-prod-01-us-west1.grafana.net/api/prom credentialsSecretRef: name: grafana-cloud # Secret labelled observability.paprika.io/credentials=true Cloud connectors (GCP and AWS) The seven cloud connectors share the same CR shape; what changes is thecredential document and the config keys: AWS (aws-cloudwatch-logs, aws-cloudwatch-metrics, aws-xray,aws-cloudtrail) — spec.credentialsSecretRef holds the same snake_caseJSON the EKS cluster provider accepts:{"access_key_id": "...", "secret_access_key": "...", "session_token": "..."}.Omit the ref entirely to use the ambient SDK chain (IRSA / IMDS /environment). Config keys: region (required), plus the connector'srequired selector (logGroup for logs, namespace for metrics), plusoptional endpoint (VPC endpoints / in-cluster emulators — the SDKsends to it verbatim) and insecureSkipTLS. GCP (gcp-cloudlogging, gcp-cloudmonitoring, gcp-cloudtrace) —the secret holds a Google credential JSON restricted to service_account,external_account or impersonated_service_account (type-checked beforeloading, same as the GKE cluster provider); omit it for ambient identity(GKE Workload Identity / metadata server). Config keys: optionalprojectId (defaults to the credential's project), optional endpoint(private proxies / fakes — replaces the *.googleapis.com base),insecureSkipTLS. Ambient identity is the gateway's own, so it is sent only to an https*.googleapis.com endpoint with TLS verification on. A provider with nocredential Secret and any other endpoint, or insecureSkipTLS, reportsNotConfigured and sends nothing; give such a provider its owncredential Secret. In external_account and impersonated_service_account documents,token_url, token_info_url and service_account_impersonation_url mustbe https *.googleapis.com URLs, universe_domain must be empty orgoogleapis.com, and credential_source.executable is refused. Thesefields decide where x/oauth2 posts subject and access tokens; it does notvalidate them itself. Empty connector queries are used internally for small health reads. Prospectivevalidate_provider and the console's Validate configuration action only checksyntax and never send credentials or make backend requests. Establish connectivityby querying an approved provider with explicit bounds. E2E coverage runs in kind: LocalStack serves CloudWatch Logs + Metrics(X-Ray and CloudTrail are license-gated there, so those two run against acanned nginx responder), and a JWT-issuing nginx fake serves the GCP RESTshapes with a runtime-generated service-account key — seetest/e2e/observabilitycloud_test.go. Enabling the gateway Check the installed release and source chart versions before upgrading the mainrelease. When the installed chart is newer, use the separategateway-only Helm add-on to preserve its controllersand resources. Its render-only helper emits three resources and keeps publicrouting disabled unless explicitly requested and approved. helm upgrade paprika-e2e charts/chart/ \ --namespace paprika-e2e --values deploy/test-values.yaml \ --values deploy/omega-values.yaml \ --set observabilityGateway.enabled=true --wait --timeout 5m Preconditions enforced at render time (helm template fails otherwise):deploymentMode: split, auth.enabled, a non-emptyPAPRIKA_AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET via observabilityGateway.extraEnv(From), andmcp.publicURL. A preconfigured OAuth client is optional for the gateway: leaveboth mcp.oauth.clientId and mcp.oauth.redirectUris empty for dynamicregistration only, or provide both for an approved static client. Partialconfiguration is rejected. Rendering and DCR-only startup configure no persistentclient; native OAuth sign-in and client-access approval are separate actions.The shared mcp configuration fields do not require mcp.enabled: that switchcontrols the independent fleet MCP surface and may remain disabled.Public exposure reuses the api-server's Gateway/hostname: observabilityGateway: enabled: true ingress: enabled: true # HTTPRoute: path prefix /observe → gateway Service Verify: curl -s https://paprika.benebsworth.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/observe/mcp | jq . # { "resource": "https://paprika.benebsworth.com/observe/mcp", # "authorization_servers": ["https://paprika.benebsworth.com/observe"], # "scopes_supported": ["paprika:observe", "paprika:insights:write"] } # The authoring scope is present only when Insights is configured. For providers signed by a CA outside the system trust bundle, configureobservabilityGateway.additionalCACertificates as a map of .crt or .pemfilenames to public PEM CA certificates (one certificate per file). The chartcreates a ConfigMap, mounts it read-only at/etc/paprika/additional-ca-certificates, and includes its contents in thegateway pod checksum so certificate updates roll out automatically. This isgateway-wide trust for all its connectors; include only CAs approved for thatscope. Provider hostname verification remains enabled. SSL_CERT_DIR includes /etc/ssl/certs, /etc/pki/tls/certs, and the addeddirectory. The default system certificate file is unchanged.
