Do not also setSSL_CERT_DIR in observabilityGateway.extraEnv; the chart rejects ambiguousconfiguration. Private keys and provider credentials belong in their existingSecret references, never in this public certificate map. Omitting the map leavesthe gateway's default trust configuration unchanged. Autodiscovery from in-cluster Services Backends running in the same cluster can register themselves without anyonehand-writing provider YAML. The provider-discovery controller(internal/controller/observe) watches Services carrying the opt-inannotation and materializes each as an ObservabilityProvider CR in theService's namespace. It runs in the observability gateway pod itself (adedicated controller-runtime manager alongside the MCP server, singlereplica with leader election off), so discovery works even where only theobservability microservice is installed; the pipeline manager alsoregisters the reconciler, and dual-running converges safely: metadata: annotations: observability.paprika.io/discover: "true" Type and endpoint are inferred from the Service: the connector type comesfrom the Service name (prometheus, loki, tempo, otel substrings — soprometheus-operated, loki-gateway, tempo-query-frontend, andotel-collector all just work), the port from each type's well-known portnames (http-web/web/http, http-metrics, otlp-http, …) falling backto the first declared port, and the endpoint ishttp://<service>.<ns>.svc:<port>. Inference overrides: Annotation Effect observability.paprika.io/type explicit connector type (prometheus/loki/tempo/otlp) when the name matches nothing observability.paprika.io/port explicit port number (invalid values hard-reject the Service) observability.paprika.io/path base path appended to the endpoint (e.g. Prometheus behind /prometheus) Ownership rules keep the CR-as-system-of-record invariant: Discovered CRs are labeled observability.paprika.io/discovered: serviceand owned by the Service — deleting the Service or removing theannotation garbage-collects the provider. The controller converges type/endpoint drift on labeled CRs but nevertouches a CR without the label — dropping the label from a discoveredprovider hands it to the operator permanently, and an operator-written CRof the same name is never deleted or modified. Discovered providers have no credentials (in-cluster backends are usuallyunauthenticated); edit the CR to add credentialsSecretRef (to a labelledSecret) and it still converges endpoint changes around your edit. Example — everything kube-prometheus-stack + loki + tempo need: kubectl annotate svc prometheus-operated -n monitoring observability.paprika.io/discover=true kubectl annotate svc loki-gateway -n monitoring observability.paprika.io/discover=true kubectl annotate svc tempo-query-frontend -n tracing observability.paprika.io/discover=true kubectl get observabilityproviders -A Provider status The gateway is also the writer behind the provider board's STATE column: itsstatus prober re-runs the catalog's per-type health probe — the cheapest readeach backend accepts, the same probe the onboarding wizard's Testconnection runs — against every registered provider on--obs-provider-probe-interval (chart observabilityGateway.probeInterval,default 5m; 0 disables status writes) and patches the verdict onto eachCR's status: state (OK/NotConfigured/NotAvailable/Error/Forbidden), a fixed-sentence reason that never carries credential orendpoint detail, observedGeneration, and a Ready condition mirroring thestate. The probe resolves credentials through the same path a query does, sostatus shows what a query would experience right now; kubectl get observabilityproviders and the console's provider board read the samefields. Managing providers in the console The dashboard's Observability page (/dashboard/observability/, listedunder Sources in the sidebar) renders three boards: Provider library — every provider type the gateway can connect to(OSS + GCP + AWS), served from the gateway's catalog: vendor, category,signals, and a one-line summary per type. Providers — every ObservabilityProvider (name, type, signals,endpoint, state, discovery provenance). Discovered providers carry aDISCOVERED pill; states map to the console's status tones. Tool usage — per-tool call/error counters maintained by the gateway'susage tracker and served from its authenticated /observe/api/usageendpoint. The api-server proxies it over GetObservabilityUsage (mintinga short-lived paprika-observability token per call); when the gateway isnot deployed the board renders the canonical "not configured" sentenceinstead of zeros. Selecting Set up on a library card opens the onboarding wizard. ItsValidate configuration action calls ValidateObservabilityProvider for offlinesyntax checks and does not establish backend access. Create provider is aseparate administrative operation that creates the provider CR and, when explicitlysupplied through the secure administration flow, its credential Secret. Creationrequires the console's write action on observabilityproviders in the targetnamespace. Workload identity avoids a static credential document. The same data is available programmatically:PaprikaService.ListObservabilityProviderTypes,GetObservabilityProviderType, ValidateObservabilityProvider,CreateObservabilityProvider, ListObservabilityProviders, andGetObservabilityUsage. On the MCP surface, agents get list_provider_types,describe_provider_type, and validate_provider alongside the query tools. Linking providers to Applications (future) The v1 CRD is deliberately shaped for a follow-up binding CR(DataProviderBinding-style scope precedence: application > namespace >cluster) that will attach providers to Applications so the console view layerand deployment pages can surface logs/metrics/traces per app. The gatewayitself is agnostic to that: tools already accept any namespace/name provider. Files cmd/main_observability_gateway.go — the --mode=observability-gateway runner internal/observabilitygateway/ — backend (CR + credential resolution), MCP tools, catalog/validate HTTP handlers, consent page, New(providerType) connector registry internal/observabilitygateway/connector/ — connector framework + registry internal/observabilitygateway/connector/{prometheus,loki,tempo,otlp}/ — the OSS connectors internal/observabilitygateway/connector/{awscommon,awscloudwatchlogs,awscloudwatchmetrics,awsxray,awscloudtrail}/ — AWS connectors (SDK v2, snake_case key JSON or ambient chain) internal/observabilitygateway/connector/{gcpcommon,gcpcloudlogging,gcpcloudmonitoring,gcpcloudtrace}/ — GCP connectors (x/oauth2 service-account/external_account/impersonated JSON or ambient, hand-rolled REST) internal/observabilitygateway/catalog/ — the provider-type library (metadata, config-field specs, onboarding steps, probes) internal/api/mcp/ — the shared MCP server (route prefix / audience / scope generalization lives here) api/observability/v1alpha1/ — the ObservabilityProvider CRD internal/webhook/observability/v1alpha1/ — admission validation charts/chart/templates/observability-gateway/ — Deployment/Service/HTTPRoute/HPA/VPA/PDB Dashboard and query integration Paprika Insights consumes the same authorized provider backend as the MCP tools.The gateway exposes GET /observe/api/providers, POST /observe/api/query andPOST /observe/api/explore for this integration. These routes require anObserve-audience bearer token and paprika:observe, then enforce the caller'snamespace RBAC before reading providers or credential Secrets. HTTP and MCPrequests share the connector concurrency budget and bounded response limits. The query route accepts a canonical namespace/name provider, signal, nativequery, RFC3339 start/end, optional stepSeconds, limit and supported paginationfields. Windows are bounded to 31 days; metrics steps must be at least onesecond and produce at most 11,000 points. query_metrics accepts the equivalentstep_seconds argument. Native response JSON and explicit provider outcomestates are preserved. Exploration adds bounded metric series and Tempo tags,including truncation indicators, for label cardinality and editor completion. Insights only advertises Prometheus and Tempo adapters, maintains stable IDsfrom the full provider namespace/name, and normalizes results for existingwidgets. Its API proxy mints a 30-second token for the authenticated human;it never queries as a shared service account. OAuth authorization and refreshalso retain exact group membership. See theInsights integration guide.

title: Use dashboard examples with real data
description: Explore Paprika Insights examples, map their queries to connected providers, and inspect live results without a sample-data fallback.
text: Shorted and Uptime dashboard examples Open Insights → Examples to browse the repository library. It contains theseven Shorted Grafana dashboards, Shorted's application dashboards, Uptime'sOverview, SLO and Reliability dashboards, a Shorted widget collection and aPaprika signal-interaction example: 16 entries and 153 sample widgets in total. The gallery records source paths, revisions, query mappings and adaptationlimits. The coverage inventoryaccounts for every source Grafana target and the application dashboard regions.These are native Paprika adaptations; source-specific controls and presentationdifferences are documented alongside each entry. Explore locally Open /dashboard/insights/?example=1. A fresh browser example workspace includesthe whole library under Repository examples. Existing edited workspaces arepreserved; use Examples to import another entry. Samples are explicitlylabelled and use local fixture data without contacting providers. The housing examples include the source's authored historical data and formulas,with their original dates. Those are static source-backed examples, not livetelemetry. Other sample data is illustrative. Connect live data Configure the required provider on Observability, using the providercatalog's field and credential guidance. Existing Prometheus and Tempoproviders remain usable. In the live Insights workspace, open Examples, choose a dashboard andreview Adaptations and data requirements. Map every placeholder to a connected provider of the matching type. Reviewthe dashboard and saved-query conflicts, then import. Imports preserve thenormal Keep/Copy/Replace choices and ETag checks. Select dashboard variables and inspect the returned data. Empty, unavailableand partial results remain visible; no live query falls back to sample data. Application and database sources use these adapters: Source Adapter and access Shorted RPC, market and news data Shorted, with fixed read operations and optional public-source credentials Shorted admin dashboard Shorted with a separate authorized adminToken; fixed GET reads only Uptime application dashboards Uptime, with organization membership and a bearer or Firebase refresh credential Shorted SQL dashboards PostgreSQL, with a dedicated SELECT-only reader and verified TLS Selecting a provider does not provision source credentials or database grants.The PostgreSQL adapter rejects privileged writer/admin roles. A private databasecertificate authority must be trusted by the gateway runtime. Source metricnames, tables and permissions must exist at the selected destination. Saved queries, widgets and MCP Application queries use a JSON operation editor. PostgreSQL uses a SQL editorwith separate typed bindings; dashboard variables belong in the binding array,while SQL contains $1, $2, and so on. Record previews offer tables, cards,treemaps, matrices, line charts and bar charts with explicit column mappings. Bundles include all referenced saved queries and can be downloaded as portableJSON. Imported documents use the same storage as Paprika Observe MCP. Discoverproviders with list_insights_providers, inspect authoring shapes withget_insights_schema, and create or patch saved queries and dashboards withthe existing authoring tools. Updates require the current ETag and synchronizewith clean UI views without overwriting unsaved drafts. Use query_records to read a provider's typed rows. Use query_dashboard tocollect a saved dashboard's bound queries once and receive compact signals.Record summaries include a bounded preview, the returned-row count, andseparate provider/summary truncation indicators. A returned page count is notthe source's total inventory count. Verification Run the repository gallery browser suite against a local UI: cd ui node e2e/run-insights.mjs e2e/insights-repository-examples.e2e.mjs It renders every sample widget in light/dark modes, checks overflow and runtimeerrors, validates portable query closure, and verifies that sample mode makesno live provider requests. The application-records suite additionally runs theObserve → Insights → UI flow with a real isolated PostgreSQL database. Itsrequired local database setting is documented inui/e2e/insights-application-records.e2e.mjs.

title: Monitor Paprika metrics and alerts
description: Read controller, drift, prune and delivery metrics, configure Prometheus scraping, and adapt alert rules to your installation.
text: Metrics and Alerting Prometheus metrics exposed by the Paprika controller-manager and how to usethem for monitoring and alerting. Accessing Metrics The controller-manager metrics port defaults to 8443. The transport followsthe Helm chart's metrics.secure value, not the port number: Chart setting Transport and access metrics.secure: true (default) HTTPS with authentication and authorization. The scraper needs permission to get the /metrics non-resource URL. metrics.secure: false HTTP; the chart passes --metrics-secure=false to the controller. Use the setting from your installed release. For HTTPS, configure the scraper'sbearer credential and certificate trust; the chart creates a<release>-metrics-reader ClusterRole that can be bound to the scraper's ServiceAccount.A local port-forward does not bypass authorization. If Prometheus Operator is installed, prometheus.enable: true renders aServiceMonitor whose port name and scheme follow metrics.secure. Review thechart's ServiceMonitor templatefor its certificate and bearer-token configuration, and themetrics-reader rolefor the permission it grants. Local HTTP example The following example applies only to an installation explicitly configuredwith metrics.secure: false. It uses the release paprika in namespacepaprika-system; substitute your own release and namespace. Keep this commandrunning in one terminal: kubectl -n paprika-system port-forward \ svc/paprika-controller-manager-metrics-service 8443:8443 Then query it from another terminal: curl --fail --silent --show-error http://localhost:8443/metrics An HTTP ServiceMonitor or PodMonitor must also use the http scheme. Do notcopy that scrape configuration to a release using secure metrics. Metric Reference Application Lifecycle Metric Type Labels Description paprika_application_phase_total Counter application, namespace, phase Application phase transitions paprika_application_reconcile_duration_seconds Histogram application, namespace Application reconciliation duration paprika_release_phase_total Counter release, namespace, phase Release phase transitions paprika_pipeline_phase_total Counter pipeline, namespace, phase Pipeline phase transitions Drift and Sync Metric Type Labels Description paprika_out_of_sync Gauge app, namespace Current out-of-sync resource count paprika_prunable Gauge app, namespace Current prunable resource count paprika_prune_total Counter app, namespace, kind Resources pruned per apply These are updated on every diff evaluation (every poll interval, default60s). The gauges reflect the CURRENT state; the counter accumulates overtime. Reconciliation Metric Type Labels Description paprika_reconcile_total Counter controller, result Controller reconciliation count paprika_reconcile_duration_seconds Histogram controller Controller reconciliation duration Sync Operations Metric Type Labels Description paprika_sync_duration_seconds Histogram app Manifest apply duration paprika_sync_errors_total Counter app Manifest apply errors Control-Plane Health These OTel instruments answer "is Paprika itself healthy and keeping up?".They are exported by the controller-manager and are the raw data behind thepaprika health CLI, the get_system_health MCP tool, andPaprikaService.GetSystemHealth. Metric Type Labels Description paprika_controller_last_reconcile_timestamp_seconds Gauge controller, result Unix timestamp of the last reconcile attempt paprika_application_last_reconcile_timestamp_seconds Gauge application, namespace Unix timestamp of the last Application reconcile attempt paprika_application_reconcile_lag Gauge application, namespace Spec generations behind the controller's observed generation paprika_applications_stale Gauge — Applications whose observed generation is behind their spec generation paprika_applications_release_retries_exhausted Gauge — Applications holding the ReleaseRetriesExhausted condition paprika_releases_stuck Gauge — Non-terminal, non-gated releases older than 30 minutes paprika_fleet_index_degraded Gauge — 1 when the fleet index health is degraded Useful queries: # Controllers that have not completed a reconcile in five minutes. # Controllers record result="success", "error", or "fail" (releases only); only success counts. time() - max by (controller) ( paprika_controller_last_reconcile_timestamp_seconds{result="success"} ) > 300 # Applications with unreconciled spec changes. max by (application, namespace) (paprika_application_reconcile_lag) > 0 # Workqueue backlog and oldest unfinished work (controller-runtime). max by (controller) (workqueue_depth) > 0 max by (controller) (workqueue_unfinished_work_seconds) > 60 max by (controller) (workqueue_longest_running_processor_seconds) > 60 # Releases that have not reached a terminal phase. paprika_releases_stuck > 0 A ready-made Insights dashboard charts these gauges with the same max()semantics as the alert rules: the paprika-control-plane starter ininternal/insights/starters/. workqueue_* and controller_runtime_reconcile_* are supplied bycontroller-runtime; the Paprika-specific gauges above add the per-applicationlag and release-liveness view that those generic metrics cannot express. OTel Instruments These use the OTel API (otel.Meter("paprika")) and appear with theotel_scope_name="paprika" label: Metric Type Description paprika_render_total Counter Template render operations paprika_render_errors_total Counter Template render errors paprika_render_duration_seconds Histogram Template render duration paprika_git_operations_total Counter Git source operations paprika_git_errors_total Counter Git source errors paprika_git_duration_seconds Histogram Git source operation duration paprika_auth_attempts_total Counter Authentication attempts paprika_auth_failures_total Counter Authentication failures paprika_authz_denials_total Counter Authorization denials paprika_sse_connections UpDownCounter Active SSE connections paprika_events_published_total Counter Events published Satellite Reporting The central API records these OTel instruments for outbound satellite reports.Prometheus translates the dotted names to underscores and adds its standardcounter and unit suffixes. OTel instrument Type Attributes Description paprika.satellite.reports Counter transport, outcome Reports by transport (post, stream) and outcome (accepted, resync, rejected) paprika.satellite.report.duration Histogram (seconds) transport, outcome Time to authenticate and persist a report paprika.satellite.report.bytes Histogram (bytes) none Uncompressed size of accepted reports paprika.satellite.link.events Counter event Link lifecycle: attached, detached, refused paprika.satellite.tasks Counter action, outcome Dispatched tasks by outcome (ok, failed, offline, error) paprika.satellite.task.duration Histogram (seconds) action Round-trip duration of a dispatched task paprika.satellite.link.up Gauge namespace, cluster Present with value 1 while a cluster holds a link paprika.satellite.report.age Gauge (seconds) namespace, cluster Time since the last accepted report; absent before the first one paprika.satellite.applications Gauge namespace, cluster Applications in the last accepted report The two transports report separately because they fail separately: a link thatstops accepting reports and a POST endpoint returning 401 are differentincidents. outcome="resync" is not a failure — the control plane is asking thesatellite to open a new session. Report age is the signal that a satellite went quiet. The fleet view keepsserving the last accepted report, so nothing else in the process knows how oldit is. link.up covers the case where the connection is gone but the age hasnot crossed the alert threshold yet; the series is absent when no link exists. # A satellite that has not reported in five minutes. paprika_satellite_report_age_seconds > 300 # Link churn: more than three detaches in ten minutes. sum(increase(paprika_satellite_link_events_total{event="detached"}[10m])) > 3 # Refused handshakes mean a credential or cluster-identity problem. increase(paprika_satellite_link_events_total{event="refused"}[15m]) > 0 Name suffixes follow the exporter's conventions: counters end in _total andgauges with unit 1 end in _ratio. See themulti-cluster guide for heartbeat and timeout settings. Kubernetes Gauges These are observable gauges populated from the K8s API on each scrape: Metric Type Description paprika_applications_active_ratio Gauge Number of active applications paprika_applications_by_phase_ratio Gauge Applications by phase paprika_releases_active_ratio Gauge Number of active releases paprika_releases_by_phase_ratio Gauge Releases by phase Note: The _ratio suffix is the OTel Prometheus exporter's convention fordimensionless (unit "1") observable gauges. Not a bug. Kubernetes Client (rest_client_*) Client-go REST metrics are exposed on every component's /metrics endpoint,filtered to the rest_client_ prefix from the component-base legacy registry: Metric Type Description rest_client_requests_total Counter Requests by code/host/method rest_client_request_duration_seconds Histogram Per-request latency rest_client_rate_limiter_duration_seconds Histogram Client-side throttle wait — sustained sum/count growth means QPS/Burst is the bottleneck rest_client_transport_cache_entries Gauge Shared transport pool size All Paprika REST configs are tuned to QPS=50 / Burst=100 (client-go defaultsare 5/10, which throttles uncached calls under load). Alerting Rules The alerts Paprika ships are inprometheusrules.yaml,enabled with prometheus.rules.enabled. That template is the source of truth.Its expressions are checked by promtool unit tests incharts/chart/tests/prometheus, and thePromQL in this guide is checked against the Go instrument definitions byinternal/metrics. The drift, prune, sync, render, git and info examples beloware illustrations, not shipped rules. Counters are created on their first increment, so a bare increase() missesthat first event. The phase alerts below pair increase() with a check for aseries with no sample in the hour before the last five minutes, and a rise abovethe value from before the last five minutes. The other increase() examples inthe Info, Warning and Drift sections do not, and can miss a first error or firstprune. Current state comes from the *_by_phase_ratio gauges. The phase alerts have one known blind spot. After an in-place container restart(same pod name and label set), the first failure of a release that the previouscontainer exported within the past hour is not reported. The new counter startsat 1, which is not above the old value, and the old samples count as history.Later failures alert through increase(). Only a drop from a higher value seenwithin about three minutes of the old container's last scrape alerts, briefly. Critical Alerts groups: - name: paprika-critical rules: # A release failed: a transition counter, transition-aware for the first event. - alert: PaprikaReleaseFailed expr: | increase(paprika_release_phase_total{phase="Failed"}[5m]) > 0 or paprika_release_phase_total{phase="Failed"} unless last_over_time(paprika_release_phase_total{phase="Failed"}[1h] offset 5m) or paprika_release_phase_total{phase="Failed"} > last_over_time(paprika_release_phase_total{phase="Failed"}[1h] offset 5m) for: 1m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "Release {{ $labels.release }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} failed" # Release retries exhausted. The gauge counts applications holding the # condition; it is unlabelled, so the alert cannot name the application. # max() collapses the same value reported by each manager pod. - alert: PaprikaReleaseRetriesExhausted expr: max(paprika_applications_release_retries_exhausted) > 0 for: 5m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "{{ $value }} application(s) hold the ReleaseRetriesExhausted condition" Warning Alerts groups: - name: paprika-warning rules: # Current state from the phase gauge, debounced for five minutes. - alert: PaprikaApplicationDegraded expr: max(paprika_applications_by_phase_ratio{phase="Degraded"}) > 0 for: 5m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "{{ $value }} application(s) are Degraded" # Rolled back: a transition counter, transition-aware for the first event. - alert: PaprikaApplicationRolledBack expr: | increase(paprika_application_phase_total{phase="RolledBack"}[5m]) > 0 or paprika_application_phase_total{phase="RolledBack"} unless last_over_time(paprika_application_phase_total{phase="RolledBack"}[1h] offset 5m) or paprika_application_phase_total{phase="RolledBack"} > last_over_time(paprika_application_phase_total{phase="RolledBack"}[1h] offset 5m) for: 1m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Application {{ $labels.application }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} was rolled back" # Drift detected and persisting - alert: PaprikaDriftDetected expr: paprika_out_of_sync > 0 for: 5m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Application {{ $labels.app }} has {{ $value }} out-of-sync resources" description: "Check kubectl get application {{ $labels.app }} -n {{ $labels.namespace }} -o json | jq '[.status.resources[] | select(.status!=\"Synced\")]'" # Prunable resources accumulating - alert: PaprikaPrunableAccumulation expr: paprika_prunable > 0 for: 10m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Application {{ $labels.app }} has {{ $value }} prunable resources" description: "Enable syncOptions.prune or review status.prunableResources" # Unexpected prune activity - alert: PaprikaUnexpectedPrune expr: increase(paprika_prune_total[5m]) > 5 labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Application {{ $labels.app }} pruned {{ $value }} resources in 5m" # Sync errors - alert: PaprikaSyncErrors expr: increase(paprika_sync_errors_total[5m]) > 0 labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Application {{ $labels.app }} had sync errors in the last 5m" # Render errors - alert: PaprikaRenderErrors expr: increase(paprika_render_errors_total[5m]) > 0 labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Template render errors in the last 5m" # Git source errors - alert: PaprikaGitErrors expr: increase(paprika_git_errors_total[5m]) > 0 labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Git source errors in the last 5m" Info Alerts groups: - name: paprika-info rules: # New application created - alert: PaprikaNewApplication expr: increase(paprika_application_phase_total{phase="Healthy"}[1h]) > 0 labels: severity: info annotations: summary: "Application {{ $labels.application }} became Healthy" Grafana Dashboards Application Health Panel { "title": "Application Health", "targets": [ { "expr": "paprika_out_of_sync", "legendFormat": "{{ app }} ({{ namespace }})" } ], "type": "stat", "fieldConfig": { "defaults": { "thresholds": { "steps": [ {"color": "green", "value": 0}, {"color": "yellow", "value": 1}, {"color": "red", "value": 5} ] } } } } Prune Activity Panel { "title": "Prune Activity", "targets": [ { "expr": "increase(paprika_prune_total[5m])", "legendFormat": "{{ app }}/{{ kind }}" } ], "type": "timeseries" } Phase Transition Timeline { "title": "Phase Transitions", "targets": [ { "expr": "increase(paprika_application_phase_total[1h])", "legendFormat": "{{ application }} → {{ phase }}" } ], "type": "timeseries" } Debugging with Metrics "Is my app drifting?" curl -s http://localhost:8443/metrics | grep 'paprika_out_of_sync{app="<app>"' If > 0, check which resources are out of sync: kubectl get application <app> -n <ns> -o json | \ jq '[.status.resources[] | select(.status!="Synced")]' "Is prune working?" curl -s http://localhost:8443/metrics | grep 'paprika_prune_total' If the counter is 0 and you expect prunes, check that syncOptions.prune isenabled on the Application. "Why is my app stuck?" curl -s http://localhost:8443/metrics | \ grep 'paprika_application_phase_total{application="<app>"' Look for transitions to Degraded, RolledBack, or Pending. Then checkthe Application conditions: kubectl get application <app> -n <ns> -o json | \ jq '[.status.conditions[] | select(.status=="True")]' "How long do syncs take?" curl -s http://localhost:8443/metrics | \ grep 'paprika_sync_duration_seconds' The histogram buckets show the distribution of apply durations per app.

title: Render dashboards for visual verification
description: Deploy the optional private browser worker and inspect saved dashboards at different viewport sizes without replacing live data checks.
text: Optional Paprika Observe browser renderer The render_dashboard MCP tool can return a real Chromium/Playwright PNGwith image/png content when an isolated render worker is configured.It captures the actual Insights UI in a loopback-only sidecar of theobservability gateway Pod. Chart installations leave it disabled by default;the trusted master publication and VKE deployment workflow enables the testedworker using the exact published image digest. Build the opt-in image with: docker build -f ui/Dockerfile.render-worker -t ghcr.io/paprikacd/paprika-render-worker:<revision> . node --test ui/render-worker.test.mjs Gateway config: PAPRIKA_OBSERVE_RENDER_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9081/render PAPRIKA_OBSERVE_RENDER_SECRET from a Kubernetes secret (32+ bytes) Renderer config: PAPRIKA_RENDER_SECRET: same secret (never log or store in Git) PAPRIKA_RENDER_UI_ORIGIN: the trusted internal Paprika UI origin,e.g. http://paprika-e2e-api-server:3000 No external Service or Ingress should expose port 9081. The MCP gatewayvalidates the dashboard through the human-authorized Insights API first,then mints a short-lived delegated token. The worker accepts only a fixeddashboard ID and viewport, blocks arbitrary browser destinations, deniesmutating API requests and wipes its ephemeral browser context after capture.All HTTP redirects are rejected before following them, including redirectsfrom an otherwise permitted API path. The gateway sends the authorizeddashboard ETag, and the worker checks the revision actually read by the UIbefore returning the PNG. A changed or unobserved revision is rejected.Browser screenshots are capped at 4 MiB, 20 seconds and two simultaneous jobs.Timeouts and client disconnects release capacity, including requests with astalled body or browser startup. Deferred widgets must finish loading beforecapture; a loading skeleton is not accepted as a completed screenshot.Every capture also runs the visual checks: DOM heuristics for clipped text,internal scroll, empty plots, widget errors and page overflow. A widget error ora failed query is a finding on its own widget, and the capture still returnswith a failed visualStatus. A failed document or listing read, a deadline or arevision change still fails the capture. checks_only returns the findings andtimings without an image.With focus_widget, the worker selects a recorded observation in an interactivechart and pins its inspector before capture. A widget without available chartinspection returns an error instead of an ordinary unfocused screenshot. The required browser CI job runs ui/e2e/insights-render-worker.e2e.mjsagainst the authenticated Insights UI with deterministic telemetry. It capturesdesktop (1512) and mobile (390) in both themes, focused plot inspection,redirect isolation, revision conflicts and provider denial, and verifies thatrendering leaves the saved document unchanged. PNGs and revision evidence areuploaded under artifacts/insights/render-worker. Those fixtures verify therenderer; production appearance still requires a live render_dashboard call.The tool is registered only when the sidecar configuration is present. Usequery_dashboard alongside the image to verify values, missing telemetry andfreshness separately. Trusted publication and VKE deployment After the required checks pass on a trusted master push, the existing publishjob builds both the application and ui/Dockerfile.render-worker. It passeseach immutable GHCR digest to the VKE reusable workflow. That workflow validatesthe renderer reference before privileged operations, then callshack/prepare-dashboard-renderer.sh in the verified vke context. The helper creates a dedicated random shared Secret only if it is absent,validates an existing Secret without printing its contents, and writes temporaryHelm values containing only the digest, Secret reference and internal UI origin.The chart grants the gateway Pod egress to this release's API server on TCP 3000.After the normal rollout checks, deployment verifies the worker's loopbackhealth endpoint inside the gateway Pod. Publication and health do not replacethe final authenticated screenshot check. Manual application deployments may omit render_worker_image_ref; the helperpreserves an already deployed immutable worker image. If no worker is deployed,that manual path leaves it disabled. It never substitutes an unpinned tag. Helm activation (after real-browser verification) An optional chart field observabilityGateway.renderWorker renders theloopback Chromium sidecar, enables the Go MCP tool and injects a pre-existingKubernetes Secret into both containers. It stays disabled by default.Enable only with a tested, immutable GHCR image digest, a private Secret andthe internal UI origin. The gateway Pod's network policy must permit egressto the selected Paprika API-server UI Service on TCP 3000. Runhelm template and inspect the Pod SecurityContext/egress rules beforedeployment; never disable network policy or reuse OAuth signing secretsas the renderer shared secret. observabilityGateway: renderWorker: enabled: true image: ghcr.io/paprikacd/paprika-render-worker@sha256:<verified-image-digest> uiOrigin: http://paprika-e2e-api-server:3000 secretName: paprika-dashboard-renderer secretKey: secret For installations outside the trusted VKE workflow, publish the worker imageand provision the dedicated Secret before enabling these values. The Helm chartitself does not create the shared Secret. Verify the deployed digest and run anauthenticated screenshot check after rollout.

title: Connect an MCP client to Paprika
description: Configure Codex, Claude Code or another MCP client for your Paprika server and complete the native OAuth sign-in flow.
text: Connect an agent to Paprika Paprika exposes fleet inspection and delivery tools through remote MCP overHTTP. An MCP client connects to an existing Paprika server; connecting does notinstall an operator or create a fleet. In this guide, https://paprika.example.com/mcp is a placeholder. Replace itwith the MCP endpoint supplied by the administrator of your Paprika installation. Connect your client Codex codex mcp add paprika --url https://paprika.example.com/mcp codex mcp login paprika Complete the native browser OAuth flow, review the requested scopes, then starta new chat. Ask for a read first: “Show fleet status and any unhealthyapplications.” Claude Code claude mcp add --scope user --transport http paprika https://paprika.example.com/mcp claude mcp login paprika Complete the native browser OAuth flow and review the requested scopes beforeasking for fleet status. Other remote MCP clients Add a remote HTTP MCP server using your installation's /mcp endpoint. Theclient needs to support Paprika's OAuth 2.1 / PKCE flow. Follow its native sign-inand consent screens; do not paste access tokens into a chat or configurationsnippet. A setup prompt you can adapt is: Connect this app to the remote MCP endpointhttps://paprika.example.com/mcp. Use the app's native OAuth flow so I can signin and review scopes. Do not ask me to paste tokens. After connecting, callfleet_status once and report the result. Use the shipped skill and plugin The repository ships one Paprika skillwith practical sequences for fleet health, drift diagnosis, release and rolloutinspection, pipeline runs, gates and controlled actions. TheClaude and Codex plugin manifests bundle this skill withan MCP server definition. The shipped plugin currently targets Ben's hosted fleet athttps://paprika.benebsworth.com/mcp. That endpoint requires access to thatinstallation; it is not an endpoint for a newly created personal fleet. See theconnector README for its documented clientcommands. For Claude Code, a local repository checkout can load the plugin with: claude --plugin-dir /absolute/path/to/paprika/plugins/paprika For your own installation, use the direct MCP routes above. If adapting a localplugin copy, review both .mcp.json and theskill's endpoint instructions so they point to the same intended server. Install Observe as a plugin without a manual clone With Node.js 20+ and the selected agent CLI installed, use the GitHub-backednpx installer: npx --yes --package=github:paprikacd/paprika -- paprika-plugins install observe --client codex # For Claude Code: use --client claude This installs paprika-observe@paprika with its skill and registers thePaprika marketplace, instead of registering only a raw endpoint. Restartthe client, finish native OAuth with paprika:observe, and calllist_observability_providers. Saved-query and dashboard authoring needsa separate paprika:insights:write grant and Insights RBAC. ChatGPT uses a different setup: register the HTTPS/observe/mcp endpoint as a custom MCP app and complete OAuth there.npx cannot register a ChatGPT app or grant access on the user's behalf.See the Observe plugin guide. Choose access deliberately paprika:read permits inspection: fleet health and topology, applications,managed resources and logs, releases, rollouts, pipeline runs and clusters.Cost queries require a configured cost source. paprika:write permits delivery actions such as sync, gate decisions,rollout controls, pipeline retry/skip/cancel and workload restart. It doesnot include read access; grant both scopes if both are needed. Read access never grants write access. To change granted scopes, use theclient's native reconnect/consent flow. Rollback, rollout promotion that skipswait or analysis, abort, pipeline skip/cancel and workload restart require asecond confirmation bound to the exact action arguments. Only confirm actionsyou intend to perform. See the scope rules,action definitions andconfirmation implementation. Requirements for a self-hosted endpoint MCP is disabled by default. An administrator must configure an authenticatedinstallation before client connection: Use deploymentMode: split and explicitly enable mcp.enabled. Enable auth.enabled and supply a non-empty PAPRIKA_AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET throughthe API server's environment or secret references. Set mcp.publicURL to the externally reachable base URL, for examplehttps://paprika.example.com; clients use that URL with /mcp appended. Configure the required static mcp.oauth.clientId and non-emptymcp.oauth.redirectUris for the installation's first-party client. Runtimesetup also requires a cache for authorization codes, refresh tokens andconfirmations. These startup requirements coexist with dynamic client registration: supportedconnectors can register their own OAuth client through /mcp/register, withtheir own validated redirect URIs. They do not need to reuse the staticfirst-party client ID. Registration accepts HTTPS redirects or loopback redirectsfor local clients. Registration survives a server replacement The Helm chart defaults mcp.oauth.persistClients to true. Each enabled MCPsurface gets a separate, retained ConfigMap containing public client IDs andtheir exact redirect allowlists, bound to that surface's resource URL. The APIserver and observability gateway receive only get/update access to theirnamed registry. Missing, inaccessible or differently bound storage fails startup;it never silently switches to an empty in-memory registry. Chart upgrades retainregistered clients. Keep these ConfigMaps when restoring the installation, andreview an issuer/resource migration explicitly rather than reusing registrationsfor a different origin or surface. Client registration does not grant account access. Console authentication,consent, scopes and PKCE remain required. Authorization codes, pending consent,refresh tokens and confirmations are not persisted in these ConfigMaps. For local/test installations, leaving both --mcp-client-registry-configmap and--mcp-client-registry-namespace unset retains process-local registration. Settingonly one is invalid. In Helm, mcp.oauth.persistClients: false explicitly optsinto that transient behavior. If a connector was registered before persistence was enabled and its metadatahas already been lost, persistence cannot reconstruct it. Use the client'ssupported registration/reconnect flow to obtain a new registration. Do notwhitelist an unknown client, broaden its redirect URI, disable PKCE or copy anaccess token into chat. A consent request rejected after successful Googlesign-in may indicate a lost client registration rather than a failed login.Check the native connector and server diagnostics separately before retrying. The registry accepts at most 4,096 clients and a bounded data size below theConfigMap limit. Exhaustion rejects new registrations without evicting existingclients. Investigate registration churn and review stale public metadata beforeany cleanup; do not delete the registry to clear a connection error. Persist OAuth sessions across restarts Set mcp.oauth.persistSessions: true for fleet MCP and/orobservabilityGateway.persistSessions: true for Observe. Each enabled surfacegets its own retained Kubernetes Secret. The server stores pending authorizations, one-usecodes, rotating refresh grants and short-lived confirmations there. Entries usehashed cache keys and AES-GCM encryption derived from the existing token-signingsecret and the exact MCP resource URL. The Secret's Role grants only get andupdate on that Secret. Missing, inaccessible, misbound or undecryptablestorage fails startup; it never silently falls back to process memory. Refresh token rotation replaces the old grant and stores the successor in oneKubernetes resource-version update. Concurrent refresh attempts have one winner;an ordinary storage outage returns a retryable error instead of telling clientsto discard a valid grant. Storage is bounded, expired entries are cleared onwrites, and temporary login traffic has its own smaller capacity limit so itcannot evict existing refresh grants. The Helm chart creates an empty Secret once as a retained pre-install/upgradehook. Later upgrades leave its contents entirely to the running server; chartrendering never snapshots mutable grants into a Helm release or overwrites themwith a stale copy. Back up the Secret and the token-signing secret together.Replacing the signing secret or changing the MCP resource URL invalidates thestored sessions and requires an intentional migration or fresh consent. Do notdelete the Secret to troubleshoot authentication. First enablement: grants held only in an already running process cannot becopied into the new store through the supported OAuth interface. Plan one freshnative connection for each affected client after switching from process-localstorage. Existing access tokens can remain usable until they expire, so asuccessful tool call immediately after rollout alone does not prove that itsrefresh grant was migrated. Rollback to an in-memory build has the samelimitation. Once a client has connected against persistent storage, its grantsurvives normal gateway and API-server replacements until its refresh lifetimeexpires. Do not extract or copy credentials from a host to bypass this step. For direct configuration, set both --mcp-session-secret and--mcp-session-namespace; omitting both retains the existing cache backend.This setting does not remove the chart's replica restrictions. Review the chart settings,chart validation,runtime validation andOAuth registration implementation whenconfiguring the server. For operator installation, start with thegetting started guide.

title: Use the Paprika fleet plugin
description: Install the Paprika plugin for Codex or Claude, inspect fleet and application state, and understand permissions for delivery actions.
text: Paprika plugin for Codex and Claude Use the Paprika plugin to inspect application health, investigate faileddeployments, read workload logs, and request delivery actions from your codingagent. The package includes operational skills and a remote MCP connection tohttps://paprika.benebsworth.com/mcp. You need a Paprika login with access to theprojects you want to inspect. No local Kubernetes credentials or server buildare needed to use the hosted connection. Install the plugin Get a checkout containing the plugin and its marketplace catalogs. If youalready have the repository, run the installation commands from its root. git clone https://github.com/paprikacd/paprika.git cd paprika The marketplace is named paprika, and the plugin is named paprika, so itsinstallation identifier is paprika@paprika. Keep a local checkout in apermanent location while using it as a marketplace source. Creating or cloning the marketplace catalogs does not register the marketplacewith Codex or Claude, or install the plugin. Run the commands for your clientbelow before looking for Paprika in its plugin list. Codex From the repository root: codex plugin marketplace add . codex plugin add paprika@paprika codex plugin marketplace list codex plugin list Verify that the marketplace list includes paprika and the plugin list includespaprika@paprika as installed and enabled. In the desktop app, refresh Pluginsif its list has not updated, then start a new Codex chat.Complete the bundled Paprika connection's OAuth sign-in when prompted. Use theclient's connection controls to sign in; do not paste a bearer token into chat.Installation enables the skills and connection. A sidebar App also requiresthe deployed server's console entrypoint; seePaprika missing from the Codex sidebar. If your Codex version has no plugin command, use the endpoint-only setup belowor update the client. See OpenAI's plugin packaging and local marketplaceguide for client details. Claude Code From the repository root: claude plugin marketplace add . claude plugin install paprika@paprika --scope user claude In the new Claude Code session, run /mcp, select the Paprika connection, andauthenticate in the browser. The bundled server is called paprika_hosted;the client may display it with a plugin prefix. You can ask for Paprika inordinary language or invoke /paprika:paprika for the operational skill and/paprika:paprika-setup for connection help. For a temporary development session, load the package directly instead: claude --plugin-dir ./plugins/paprika Use the marketplace installation for normal use and --plugin-dir whenchecking local edits. See Claude Code's pluginguide and MCP authenticationguide. Endpoint-only setup and other MCP clients If you only want the tools, connect the remote server directly. This does notinstall the packaged skills. Use one Paprika connection per client; disable aduplicate direct connection when switching to the full plugin. For Codex: codex mcp add paprika_hosted --url https://paprika.benebsworth.com/mcp codex mcp login paprika_hosted --scopes paprika:read For Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http --scope user paprika_hosted https://paprika.benebsworth.com/mcp claude Then use /mcp in Claude Code to authenticate. In other MCP clients, add thesame HTTPS URL as a Streamable HTTP server and use the client's native OAuthflow. Interactive panels and the application mention picker require hostsupport; ordinary read and write tools work without those UI features. For your own Paprika instance, replace the URL in bothplugins/paprika/mcp.json and plugins/paprika/.mcp.json before installing, oruse your instance's URL in the endpoint-only commands. The server needs MCPand OAuth enabled; see the deployment section below and theauthentication guide. Sign in and verify access Inspection requires paprika:read. Delivery actions also requirepaprika:write and your existing Paprika RBAC permissions. Review the scopesin native OAuth consent; reconnect through the client when you need to changeaccess. For an endpoint-only Codex connection that needs both scopes, use: codex mcp login paprika_hosted --scopes paprika:read,paprika:write After approving access in Paprika, the capsicum screen shows add some spice,the account, deployment hostname, and granted access. Choose Continue toapplication to return to the client's validated callback and finish connecting.“Access approved” confirms the Paprika approval; the client confirms the finalconnection after exchanging the authorization code. The final localhost callbackpage is owned by Codex or Claude and cannot be styled by the Paprika server. After sign-in, start with: Use Paprika to show fleet status and applications that need attention.Include each app's namespace, reported health, and out-of-sync count. The agent should discover the server's tools, call fleet_status, and uselist_applications as needed. Check that the returned projects and namespacesmatch your access. If no applications are visible, confirm the selectedaccount and project permissions before treating the fleet as empty. The installed package and the deployed server have separate versions. Thefleet panel and composite health report require the server to exposeopen_fleet and get_application_health; discover those tools before usingthem. Earlier deployments can still provide the existing read tools. Use Paprika Include the namespace and application name in requests for one application.These are example prompts; replace production/checkout with your app. Task Prompt Fleet overview "Show Paprika fleet health and any drifted or unhealthy apps." App health "Check production/checkout. Explain health, drift, failed checks, and the current release." Deployment failure "Investigate the latest failed release for production/checkout. Show the failing resources and supporting evidence." Resource logs "Inspect the resource tree for production/checkout, then fetch the last 200 log lines for the failing workload." Interactive console "Open the Paprika fleet console for the production namespace." Requested sync "Sync production/checkout with its configured source, then check progress and report remaining gates or failures." In a host that renders MCP Apps, the console offers Health, Resources,Deployments, and Debug views. Filter the fleet by namespace or search, selectan app, and inspect conditions, checks, release failures, and resource readiness.Run an investigation or open logs when you need additional evidence. UseAttach to chat to add the selected app's context to the conversation.Request sync sends an action request to chat; completion is establishedby subsequent health and deployment checks. A reported Healthy app can still have drift or an exhausted release retrybudget. Keep those signals separate. Unknown, unavailable or stale evidence,and empty investigation findings do not establish health. Logs load on demand,and app health is reported by the controller rather than inferred from asuccessful MCP call. Troubleshoot the connection Symptom What to check Plugin or marketplace not found Catalog files alone do not register or install anything. Run the install commands from the repository root. For Codex, check codex plugin marketplace list for paprika and codex plugin list for paprika@paprika, then refresh Plugins and open a new chat. Plugin installed but tools are missing Start a new chat, confirm the plugin and bundled server are enabled, and complete OAuth. In Claude Code, inspect /mcp. Plugin installed but missing from Codex Sidebar / Apps Follow the sidebar checks below. The server must advertise the console's global entrypoint before Codex can offer it in Explore. Sign-in fails or returns 401 Reconnect through native OAuth to the exact /mcp URL. If it persists, ask the server operator to check public URL, discovery, and redirect configuration. Reads or actions are denied Check the granted read/write scopes and Paprika project RBAC. Write access does not imply read access. Console or new health tool is unavailable Check deployed tool discovery and host MCP Apps/Extensions support. Installing the package does not upgrade the server. Some evidence is missing Inspect section errors, status.partial, timestamps, and truncation markers. Use targeted resource reads and logs for the available evidence. Tools appear twice Keep either the plugin's connection or the direct MCP entry enabled. Paprika missing from the Codex sidebar Check codex plugin list for paprika@paprika as installed and enabled,and complete native OAuth for the Paprika connection. This verifies thepackage and connection; it does not create a sidebar App by itself. Ask Codex: "Discover the tools on my Paprika connection. Is open_fleetavailable?" The deployed API server must expose open_fleet with a globalMCP App entrypoint. If it is missing, the Paprika operator needs to upgradethe API server. Reinstalling the plugin package does not deploy that upgrade. After the server upgrade, open a new chat and verify tool discovery again.If Codex still lists the earlier tools, open Plugins, switch the Paprikaplugin off and back on, then start a new chat. This reloads the local pluginconfiguration without removing its saved OAuth sign-in. The Codex clientmust support MCP Apps and Extensions to offer the sidebar entry. Once Codex discovers the entrypoint, open Explore → Paprika, then choosePin to sidebar to keep it in the navigation rail. Discovered Apps arenot pinned automatically. For an existing sidebar App, its Refresh action reloads the console UI andrestarts the widget. It does not add tools that the server has not deployed. After updating the plugin source, refresh or reinstall it through the client'splugin manager and start a new session. For Claude Code's marketplace install,use claude plugin marketplace update paprika, thenclaude plugin update paprika@paprika. For Codex, refresh the marketplace andreinstall or update Paprika from Plugins. Server tools and the console bundleare updated by the Paprika operator's normal API-server deployment workflow. Package and authentication plugins/paprika/plugin.json is the portable Agent Plugins 1.0 manifest.mcp.json points to https://paprika.benebsworth.com/mcp using Streamable HTTP.Compatibility manifests and .mcp.json preserve Codex/Claude clients using theearlier package layout. Identity, branding, and default prompt order stayconsistent across the package's presentation metadata. Connect through the client's native OAuth flow. Paprika supports OAuth 2.1 withPKCE, discovery, and dynamic client registration. Inspection requirespaprika:read; writes require paprika:write and the existing RBAC permissions.The scopes are independent. The package contains no credentials or auth headers.The optional paprika-setup skill verifies access with fleet_status after login. Observability gateway Install Paprika Observe through the plugin Node.js 20+ can install the complete Codex or Claude Code plugin from theGitHub repository without a manual clone: npx --yes --package=github:paprikacd/paprika -- paprika-plugins install observe --client codex npx --yes --package=github:paprikacd/paprika -- paprika-plugins install observe --client claude The npx distribution bundles the marketplace, plugin manifests, MCP URL andObserve skill. It stages a managed marketplace under~/.paprika/plugin-marketplace, uses the selected client's plugin commands,and then asks the user to finish native OAuth. It does not create a duplicatedirect MCP entry or capture credentials. Rerun the command to refresh thestaged marketplace, then restart or refresh the client. First connection: grant paprika:observe read access, start a newconversation, and call list_observability_providers. Select an actualprovider and run a small query before claiming that live data is available.Authoring is opt-in: explicitly reconnect withpaprika:observe,paprika:insights:write and retain Insights RBAC. ChatGPT: npx cannot register a ChatGPT custom MCP app or provide aninteractive Connect control. Registerhttps://paprika.benebsworth.com/observe/mcp as a custom MCP app, completebrowser OAuth, and verify its tools. A private ChatGPT plugin can wrap thatregistered app using the real app ID in .app.json; do not commit a personalapp ID to this public repository or invent a binding. The optional paprika-observe packageconnects the separate /observe/mcp endpoint and bundles an observability skill.Its portable manifest uses streamable-http and per-server OpenAI OAuthconfiguration with DCR and paprika:observe as the default read scope;paprika:insights:write requires separate authoring consent; its supported Codex and Claude compatibilitymanifests use .mcp.json with type: "http". Version 0.3.0 advertises Read andWrite capabilities for telemetry reads and saved-query/dashboard authoring.The existing fleet package still connects only /mcp. After the user explicitly approves configuring persistent access to the exactdeployment, install paprika-observe@paprika from this repository marketplaceusing the same client commands as the fleet plugin, or use an endpoint-onlyconnection. These commands configure client access and must not be run merelyto validate package structure: codex mcp add paprika_observe --url https://YOUR_VERIFIED_PAPRIKA_HOST/observe/mcp codex mcp login paprika_observe --scopes paprika:observe For Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http paprika_observe https://YOUR_VERIFIED_PAPRIKA_HOST/observe/mcp For saved-query and dashboard authoring, request a fresh consent grant withboth scopes (and retain the user's existing Insights write permission): codex mcp login paprika_observe --scopes paprika:observe,paprika:insights:write Existing read-only tokens stay read-only on refresh. An OAuth request withoutscopes keeps the read-only default; compatibility clients need to request theauthoring scope explicitly. The deployment advertises that scope only whenInsights is configured. Authoring does not grant provider configuration orfleet writes. Then complete sign-in through /mcp in Claude Code. Use native OAuth consent;never supply copied fleet tokens or provider credentials. Each deployment andsurface has its own OAuth connection. The packaged hosted origin is a default,not evidence that it is the intended GKE deployment. First discover actual tools, call list_observability_providers, describe areturned namespace/name, and discover its metrics, labels, or trace services.Use that provider's query syntax, a short explicit time range and a small limit.Inspect state, reason, truncation and continuation fields. Provider-specificlimitations and empty results remain visible. validate_provider is an offlineconfiguration check; only a real bounded provider query validates connectivity. Paprika Insights can also consume this same Observe MCP endpoint as its datasource. With the gateway configured for Insights, open Data sources to seethe Paprika Observe MCP connection and discovered Prometheus/Tempo providers,then choose Explore. PromQL and TraceQL requests run through query_metricsand query_traces; dashboard variables, saved-query parameters and tooltipbindings are resolved before the tool call. list_metric_series supplies abounded series sample for label/cardinality inspection. The UI uses thesigned-in Paprika user's delegated read permissions, independently of an AIclient's native OAuth connection. See the Insights integration. The observe resource advertises the authorization-server issuerhttps://HOST/observe. RFC 8414 discovery therefore resolves/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/observe, independently of the fleet'sroot metadata. RFC 9728 canonical resource metadata is available at/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/observe/mcp; the explicit 401 challengealso retains /observe/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource for compatibility.Ingress must route both canonical observe metadata paths to the gateway.Its JWTs keep the deployment origin issuer and require the separatepaprika-observability audience. Shared grant-cache records also bind audience,and refresh tokens bind client ID; pre-upgrade unbound refresh records requirea fresh OAuth login. The pinned Go MCP SDK supports legacy 2025 clients and the 2026-07-28 protocol.For the modern protocol, HTTP cancellation propagates into the tool context;legacy stateless requests retain their backend timeout bound. Invalid Originheaders are rejected; native clients can omit Origin. Per-subject rate limitsinclude Retry-After. Package tests and local protocol tests establish servercontracts; they do not prove installed-client OAuth, deployed ingress, or liveprovider access. With mcp.oauth.persistClients enabled (the chart default), the gateway's DCRregistry persists in its resource-bound ConfigMap and survives restarts.Without persistent registration storage, clients must re-register after arestart. OAuth access/refresh grants and internal console delegation preservethe authenticated user's exact groups, including an explicitly empty set;subject and group RBAC apply without substituting a service identity. Neverbroaden RBAC to work around a denied query or document write. Validate without installation or new credentials: claude plugin validate --strict plugins/paprika-observe node --experimental-strip-types --test internal/api/mcp/ui/tests/observe-plugin.test.ts go test ./internal/api/mcp -count=1 These layouts and commands follow OpenAI plugin packaging,Codex MCP,Claude plugin manifests,Claude MCP, and theMCP authorization discoveryand Streamable HTTPspecifications. Do not substitute an HTTP+SSE URL or assume all host UI extensionsare supported merely because ordinary tools work. Multiple Paprika deployments Use one Paprika product plugin with separate named connections and OAuth accountsfor each origin. Keep the existing paprika_hosted connection tohttps://paprika.benebsworth.com/mcp. To connect another deployment, the Codex CLIsupports this example: codex mcp add paprika_starfleethub --url https://paprika.starfleethub.com/mcp codex mcp login paprika_starfleethub --scopes paprika:read These commands configure and authenticate a second connection; they do not deployPaprika or verify its server version, tools, permissions, or interactive UI.Authenticate each origin independently and keep its account/scopes separate.Never reuse tokens across origins or silently fall back to another connectionwhen the selected deployment is unavailable. Specify the connection plus namespace/application in requests, for example:“On paprika_starfleethub, check production/checkout.” Label comparisons andread results with their connection and endpoint; identical app names can belongto different deployments. Keep mutations and follow-up verification on theexplicitly selected connection. In the fleet console, open the instance control in the header. It shows thecurrent deployment, account display information when available, and grantedread/write scopes. The instance picker includes Personal and StarfleetHubdestinations; add other deployments with a label, named MCP connection, andendpoint. Saved destinations are preferences, not evidence that a server isconnected or healthy. Only public connection details are saved locally, andpreferences may be unavailable in hosts that block browser storage. Choose Open fleet on the destination. The console asks the conversationto verify that exact connection with get_connection and open its open_fleetview using that connection's native OAuth. If the named connection is missing,use the picker’s setup instructions. The original instance and evidence remainlabelled while the request is pending; a newly opened view confirms the target.Hosts without message support show instructions instead. This is a handoff through Codex, rather than a change to the existing iframe'stransport: the MCP Apps bridge calls only the server that opened the view.The console makes no direct requests to another origin and never moves tokensbetween deployments. Attached app context and action requests include theverified endpoint; sync requests are disabled until instance identity is known. get_connection returns this server's configured endpoint, acting account displayfields, granted scopes, and build identity. It accepts no target arguments anddoes not enumerate other connections. Deployed servers must include these sourcechanges to expose the identity tool and the new switcher. Production MCP tokenvalidation also requires an issuer matching that deployment's public URL. Interactive fleet view and app context open_fleet accepts optional namespace, search, page_size (default 50,maximum 200), and cursor. It returns fleet status and one authorized applicationpage and associates the result with ui://paprika/console. The bundledMCP App uses the host bridge to read tools, attach selected app context, and senduser-requested action messages into chat. It uses the opener's initial resultinstead of requesting it again on launch. The resource advertises fullscreen as its preferred and available display mode.Codex uses this for a side panel; placement and Extensions availability dependon host capability negotiation. The UI reports unsupported host controls andtool errors instead of presenting empty results as healthy. Namespace/searchfilters and pagination preserve scope. Only explicit investigation/log actionscollect that additional evidence, and log text is escaped before rendering. search_mentions accepts query and returns at most 20 authorized applicationlinks. Each paprika://applications/{namespace}/{name} resource resolves throughget_application_health with fresh authorization. Mentioning or attaching an appdoes not authorize a delivery action. Hosts without Extensions can continueusing ordinary MCP tools. Read an application's evidence Use get_application_health with required name and namespace. Its boundedreport includes: Controller-reported phase, health, sync counts, revisions, stage/releaseidentity, retry latch, and timestamped conditions. Health checks and SLO coverage without HTTP response bodies or timelines. Managed resource sync and health, with unhealthy/out-of-sync entries first. Recent releases, hook/policy failures, canary step/weight, and bounded explicitrollout references with readiness, pause/abort state, and workload/service refs. Drift collection state and available details, with field/page truncation. Optional application investigation when include_investigation=true. resource_limit defaults to 50 and is capped at 200; release_limit defaultsto 5 and is capped at 20. At most five linked rollouts are fetched. Sync andhealth resource lists stay separate because their current API records lackapiVersion; joining by kind/name could collapse resources from different groups.The summary excludes rendered release snapshots and rollout HTTP headers. Application access is checked first. Failure aborts the read. Secondary failuresremain visible by section and make status.partial=true; backend error detailsare logged server-side and omitted from the returned error message.observedAt is collection time, while condition/check timestamps describecontroller evidence. Missing, stale, forbidden, and unconfigured sections donot establish health or zero drift. The current detailed drift backend returnsNOT_CONFIGURED; resource sync and status.outOfSync remain available. For more detail, use get_application, get_resource_tree with detailed=true,investigate on an exact selected resource, or get_logs with tail_lines.The investigator's findings are advisory: its current API does not report eachsource collection failure. Empty findings or missing logs are not proof of anabsence of errors. Pipeline run-history collection is currently unavailable;Pipeline object status and step logs remain useful evidence. Delivery actions The console's action controls send an exact target/action request into chat.Write tools enforce scope, RBAC, and the existing two-phase confirmation forrollback, promotion, abort, step skip, pipeline cancel, and workload restart.An initial destructive call returns a preview and confirmation_token with nomutation. A confirmed call uses identical arguments plus that token. Tokens arebound to the principal, tool, and arguments and are single-use. sync_application requests reconciliation of the configured source; it does notupload a new manifest or image. Re-read state after every write and verifyrelease/rollout completion, resource health/sync, and checks before reportingdeployment success. Registered hold/resume tools currently report unimplemented;their presence in discovery does not imply they changed a rollout. Build, deployment, and verification From the repository root: make build-mcp-ui npm --prefix internal/api/mcp/ui run check npm --prefix internal/api/mcp/ui test go build ./... go test ./internal/api/mcp -count=1 go test ./internal/engine ./internal/controller/pipelines -count=1 go vet ./internal/... ./cmd/... make build-mcp-ui installs pinned dependencies and builds one self-containedHTML file embedded into the API-server binary. The bundle uses the installedMCP Apps and OpenAI Extensions SDKs; it makes no direct API fetches and declaresno external connect/resource domains. Package and UI tests check the documentedtool contracts, identity, metadata, prompt ordering, scoped pagination, races,missing evidence, error handling, and user-triggered context/actions. Source changes do not install/reload a client plugin or upgrade the hostedserver. The running endpoint serves the deployed API-server image. Build animmutable linux/amd64 image and deploy through the existing Helm workflow,after rendering the chart and confirming the configured VKE context. Verifythe intended API-server image and rollout, then discover tools/resources andopen the console in the target host. A successful JSON tool result verifiesthe server path; it does not prove the host rendered the panel or mention picker.Retain those host checks as unverified until actually exercised. The API-server deployment needs mcp.enabled=true, a valid mcp.publicURL,server auth, token signing configuration, and the configured static OAuthclient/redirect allowlist required by construction. Dynamic registrationsupports additional native clients. Never commit auth secrets or renderedmanifests containing them. See operations for the establishedbuild/deploy workflow. The integration follows OpenAI MCP Extensions,the MCP Apps protocol, andAgent Plugins 1.0.BrandBrain's existing plugin and bridge pattern informed the navigation,on-demand evidence, and explicit context/action controls.

title: Install and use Paprika Observe
description: Install the Observe plugin, connect with OAuth, discover telemetry providers, and create or update shared Insights dashboards.
text: Paprika Observe plugin One-command install (Codex / Claude Code) Requires Node.js 20+ and an installed Codex or Claude Code CLI. This GitHub-backednpx command installs the complete plugin and its skill, not just an MCP URL: npx --yes --package=github:paprikacd/paprika -- paprika-plugins install observe --client codex # Or use --client claude, or --client both The installer stages the marketplace at ~/.paprika/plugin-marketplace, registersit with the selected client, and installs paprika-observe@paprika. Rerun thecommand to refresh the staged package; restart the client or refresh its plugin.It never copies OAuth tokens or silently registers a second direct MCP entry. Complete sign-in in your client. First grant paprika:observe for read-onlytelemetry and dashboards; for Insights authoring, reconnect withpaprika:observe,paprika:insights:write and your existing Insights RBAC.Verify access with list_observability_providers, then list_dashboards andquery_dashboard. Successful installation alone is not proof of connection. ChatGPT: npx configures Codex or Claude Code; it cannot register a ChatGPTcustom MCP app or initiate browser consent on the user's behalf. In ChatGPT,add https://paprika.benebsworth.com/observe/mcp as a custom MCP app andcomplete OAuth there. To bundle that registered app into a private ChatGPTplugin, use its actual app ID in .app.json and reference it fromextensions.com.openai.apps; never guess that ID or copy another user's appbinding into this public repository. An optional plugin for Paprika's separate observability gateway. It bundlesprovider discovery, bounded telemetry queries, dashboard query bundles, andsaved-query/dashboard authoring.It does not add a connection to the existing fleet plugin automatically. The packaged endpoint is https://paprika.benebsworth.com/observe/mcp.Deployment and client access are separate: installing this source cannotdeploy the gateway or establish which providers the server can access.For GKE or another origin, select the verified deployment URL and use theendpoint-only connection instructions in the integration guide. When the user explicitly requests installation, run from the repository root: codex plugin marketplace add . codex plugin add paprika-observe@paprika Or in Claude Code: claude plugin marketplace add . claude plugin install paprika-observe@paprika --scope user Complete native OAuth for this connection with paprika:observe for reads andexplicitly consent to paprika:insights:write to create or update saved queriesand dashboards. Authoring also requires your existing Insights write permission.The server advertises the authoring scope only when Insights is configured.Existing read-only tokens stay read-only, including on refresh: update theplugin and reconnect through native OAuth to request the new scope. Clientsusing the compatibility manifest must request paprika:insights:write in theirOAuth authorization flow; a request with no scope keeps the read-only default.Never copy fleet tokens, service-account keys, or provider credentials into a manifest.Then discover tools, call list_observability_providers, select an actualprovider identity, and run a small discovery/query. Native client sign-in,real tool discovery, and real backend queries require independent validation. Validate package structure without installing or authenticating: claude plugin validate --strict plugins/paprika-observe node --experimental-strip-types --test internal/api/mcp/ui/tests/observe-plugin.test.ts Portable mcp.json uses streamable-http and the OpenAI per-server OAuthextension; compatibility .mcp.json uses http. The Codex and Claude overlayspoint to the compatibility file. No background hooks or credential scriptsare included. Read a dashboard query bundle For an existing dashboard, call list_dashboards to discover its ID, thenquery_dashboard to collect its live signals in one request: { "name": "query_dashboard", "arguments": { "id": "service-overview", "variables": { "service": "uptime-api" } } } The gateway resolves the dashboard's saved queries and parameter bindings,applies one shared time range and filter set, and executes identical queriesonce. Its compact structuredContent includes widget-to-signal references,exact readings, units, timestamps, range summaries and a small trace sample.A short text synopsis presents the bundle without duplicating the full JSON.Missing data, failed queries and truncation remain explicit. This is read-only: it requires paprika:observe plus existing Insights/providerpermissions, and never changes the dashboard's defaults. Clients do not need tofetch each saved query and execute it separately. To inspect a small trend, add"widget_ids": ["request-rate"] and "history_points": 12. The default usesthe saved dashboard range; pass both start and end for a fixed interval.Tooltip-only queries still need a hovered observation. See thedashboard query contract forlimits, result interpretation and live validation. Authoring flow Discover list_insights_providers for the actual provider IDs used by the UI.Use get_insights_schema with kind: dashboard, widget, or saved_queryfor the deployed schema, examples and semantic constraints.Read existing documents with list_saved_queries, get_saved_query,list_dashboards, and get_dashboard. Create saved queries before dashboardsthat reference them, using create_saved_query and create_dashboard.Targeted edits use patch_saved_query and patch_dashboard: nested objectsmerge, null removes a field, and arrays replace. Dashboard widget_editsadd, update or remove widgets by stable ID in one atomic save. Full-documentreplacements remain available through update_saved_query andupdate_dashboard. Every edit requires the exact ETagreturned by the last read. A conflict requires a fresh read and review of bothchanges; do not retry an overwrite with a wildcard ETag. Query provider/kindidentity and existing dashboard parameter bindings remain protected by thesame service that handles UI edits. These tools edit the shared Insights documents. An open UI refreshes externalchanges while preserving unsaved local drafts. Returned dashboard links openthe saved workspace. Authoring grants no fleet writes, provider configuration,credential management, or deletion tools. See the targeted authoring contractfor patch examples, immutable fields and limits.

title: Paprika API reference
description: Explore Paprika's Connect-RPC API for applications, releases, pipelines and related resources, with request and response examples.
text: Connect-RPC API This page documents direct Connect JSON access and selected Paprika RPCs. Thefull service definition is in proto/paprika/v1/api.proto. For access from Codex or Claude, see the Paprika plugin guide.The /mcp endpoint exposes authenticated tools for app health, debugging, anddelivery operations, with OAuth sign-in and the same application permissions asthe API. The guide covers installation, example prompts, and MCP Apps support. A second, independent MCP surface lives at /observe/mcp (the observabilitygateway). The paprika:observe scope allows authorized reads of logs, metrics,traces, and Insights documents.
